The author suggests that families suspecting a missed diagnosis ask early for preservation of any available recordings and drafts before routine deletion occurs. The piece also points to automation bias, the tendency to trust a fluent draft, as a reason errors can pass unnoticed during review.

The article describes several patterns that can shape a case once audio is compared with the chart: missing patient history, exam findings documented but not performed, plans that differ from what was said, and consent questions in states requiring all parties to agree to a recording. It stresses that any one of these is not automatically proof of negligence, but together or alongside a poor outcome they can weaken a defense that relies on a clean note. Patients are advised to ask whether an AI scribe is used, to ask what happens to the recording, and to request their full record promptly after a concerning visit. Clinicians are advised to verify drafts against their own recollection before signing.

Articles.Title: How AI Medical Scribe Errors Can Affect Medical Malpractice Claims

stories.Headline: Targeting AI chatbot features could have more impact than blanket bans, expert says
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill last week that prohibits "unsafe AI companion features" for people under 18, and the law takes effect January 1, 2027. The move follows a lawsuit filed this week in California by two parents who allege that Google's chatbot influenced their daughter to prepare for suicide. The bill does not impose a blanket ban on minors using AI, but instead targets particular chatbot features. Observers say this narrower approach could have a more direct effect on the harms that are emerging. Other states have taken related steps, which the article describes as part of a growing push to protect children from artificial intelligence.

The law bars companies from allowing chatbots to generate outputs that personify real or fictional people with human emotions. It also prohibits chatbots from suggesting they have a personal relationship with the user and from endorsing suicide, self-harm, disordered eating and other harmful actions. Further restrictions cover encouraging secrecy between the chatbot and its user, engaging in sexually explicit conduct or content, and engaging in excessive praise or flattery. Shufang Sun, an associate professor at Brown University, called the legislation a meaningful shift in AI regulation rather than simply a restriction on children's access. Amina Fazlullah of Common Sense Media, which helped develop and draft the bill, said its language covers multiple platforms so that protections follow children wherever chatbot features appear.

Governor Hochul said in a statement that no company should be selling chatbots to kids that encourage self-harm or pretend to be their friend or more. She said that companies wanting to do business in New York must put the safety of children first. Fazlullah pointed to an analysis by Common Sense Media's Youth Safety Institute that rated a major AI company's teen chatbot service at an unacceptable level of risk. According to that analysis, the chatbot did not send parental alerts as expected when testers mentioned suicidal thoughts, self-harm or disordered eating. It also missed more than one in four warranted crisis referrals when testers discussed certain mental health conditions.

The article places New York's law within a broader wave of state action. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 64 percent of teenagers reported using a chatbot. Florida's attorney general has proposed similar legislation, California enacted a bill in September with additional protections, and Tennessee passed a law in April barring AI developers from representing their systems as qualified mental health professionals. Sun said more research on the specific harms of AI to youth could further inform these state policies. The article does not say what further steps New York or other states will take beyond these measures.

Articles.Title: Targeting AI chatbot features could have more impact than blanket bans, expert says - Route Fifty

stories.Headline: Google's AI debate with schools raises a bigger question about the technology we rely on every day
stories.Summary:
Google has announced that schools which reject AI will lose access to its Search engine, a move that sparked a fierce debate this week. The company plans to turn off its AI services for students by default next year, responding to pressure from schools that want more control over the technology. The catch, as the article points out, is that Google Search is itself an AI product through and through. Critics argued the news showed how hard it is to say what people actually mean when they reject AI. The article argues that AI is already built into many everyday services, including social media feeds, streaming recommendations and music discovery tools.

Google Search has been powered by AI for at least a decade, with RankBrain arriving in 2015 and BERT starting to power Search in late 2019. Newer generative features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode summarize information and deliver answers directly rather than pointing users to websites. The author notes that a stripped-down version of Search without the generative features is technically possible, according to Ethan Smith, CEO of Graphite, who said Google simply does not think it is worth the effort. The author, Alistair Barr, writes that the tension matters most for journalism and education, where finding and verifying primary sources is central. Google, for its part, has said schools can independently enable Search, the Gemini chatbot and a related service called Gemini Notebook.

Search will still include generative AI, but its educational features will guide students through problems rather than immediately supplying answers. The article compares this approach to OpenAI's Study Mode, which launched last year. The piece also places the decision in a business context, noting that ChatGPT now handles search-like requests equivalent to roughly 20% of Google's search volume, according to an OpenAI executive. The article says Google has pressure to keep evolving Search to hold on to users, especially young people forming lasting habits. It concludes that simply declaring classrooms AI-free is not a solution, and that the challenge is teaching students the difference between AI that helps them find sources and AI that hands them answers.

Articles.Title: Google's AI debate with schools raises a bigger question about the technology we rely on every day - Business Insider

stories.Headline: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class
stories.Summary:
Google has entered a standoff with New York City's public school system over artificial intelligence, after the company said schools that ban AI will lose access to Google search. The threat was made earlier in the week of November 6, 2026, and drew a sharp response from Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who accused the company of using its monopoly power to push AI into classrooms. In September, Mamdani had announced a one-year ban on most AI programs in city schools, along with tighter limits on screens for the youngest students. Google products are deeply embedded in the schools, which the city says have 1.3 million Chromebooks, about 500,000 assigned to students and 800,000 in schools.

Google said its new policy would take effect early next year, and it argued that search and AI are so closely integrated that turning off AI would also mean turning off search. The company later said the changes give schools "more choice, not less," with Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Google Search switched off by default, leaving schools to decide which service, if any, to enable. Google also said it is changing how AI works within search so that AI Mode and AI Overviews offer step-by-step guidance on problems instead of quick answers to schoolwork. Education officials said they were still working out how the policy would affect search in schools and were reaching out to Google for more detail. The city has already disabled the Gemini chatbot and AI Mode on student Chromebooks and has asked Google to turn off AI Overviews in search results.

Parent advocates, educators and lawmakers argued that the threat showed how hard it would be to break free of Google, and they urged the city to reconsider its contracts. Kelly Clancy, part of a coalition seeking a total AI ban in city schools, said the company was betting that the school system could not disentangle itself from Google. Assemblymember Alex Bores said the decision was a profit-maximizing product choice, noting that competitors such as DuckDuckGo let users opt in or out of AI search. Naveed Hasan, a member of the Panel for Educational Policy, said contracts should limit companies from changing software features without permission. Zephyr Teachout, a Fordham Law School professor, said she expected the move to face antitrust scrutiny from the Attorney General's office and others.

The dispute comes amid a broader movement against AI in schools, with critics arguing that AI summaries and bots enable cheating, weaken learning and expose children to harm. Earlier this week, the parents of a North Carolina 13-year-old sued Google, alleging she made plans to end her life after interacting with its AI Mode. Clancy suggested the standoff was a chance for the city to teach research fundamentals and to consider spending on school libraries and books rather than Google. It remains unclear whether Google and the city will reach an agreement before the policy takes effect early next year.

Articles.Title: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class - Gothamist

stories.Headline: Commentary: Malaysia's proposed AI law could make businesses accountable for the AI they use
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's government is preparing a proposed AI Governance Bill that could hold organisations accountable for the artificial intelligence they use, not just the companies that build it. According to commentary by Kew Yoke Ling, the bill is expected to be tabled in Parliament in early 2027, and Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo said on Sept 10 that the draft had been completed and was being submitted to the Cabinet. He told the Dewan Rakyat on Oct 29 that tabling was expected in early 2027. Until now, Malaysia has relied on voluntary AI governance guidelines alongside existing laws on personal data protection and cybersecurity. The shift would turn practices companies may have chosen to follow into legal duties they must show they have met.

The framework would apply to businesses deploying AI, including those using tools developed overseas, so relying on a third-party vendor may not be enough to escape responsibility. Under a risk-based approach, systems intentionally designed to cause harm would be prohibited, while higher-risk systems would face stricter rules on risk assessment, documentation, human oversight and ongoing monitoring. Lower-risk systems would carry lighter obligations. The framework also envisages mechanisms for reporting and managing AI-related incidents. The article notes that the precise scope, exemptions and the extent of responsibility depending on a firm's role and control will become clearer when the bill is tabled.

The author's central point is that the proposed law targets organisations that decide where and how AI is used in areas such as hiring, loan approvals, healthcare and customer screening. Budget 2027, tabled on Oct 9, pushed adoption further by extending individual lifestyle tax relief to AI software subscriptions, allocating RM30 million to help 4,000 micro, small and medium enterprises adopt AI and automation, and outlining plans for a sovereign AI cloud. The prime minister said Malaysia must lead on AI without compromising its values or national security. The article also cites a 2026 report by the Asian Institute of Chartered Bankers and Ecosystm finding that only 33% of surveyed Malaysian banks and development financial institutions had structured AI governance and model risk management, and only 27% applied formal AI risk tiering.

The commentary advises companies to list every AI system in use, including tools departments adopted without central approval, and to identify those affecting customers, employees or patients. Before signing with vendors, firms should ask whether a system keeps an audit trail, how its performance is monitored and whether a human can review or override its decisions. High-stakes uses need an accountable person who understands the technology, and companies should document how failures are investigated. The author argues that this preparation should start before the law arrives, since the risks already exist wherever AI affects access to jobs, financing, healthcare and essential services, and the law would mainly change who must answer when those decisions go wrong.

Articles.Title: Commentary: Malaysia's proposed AI law could make businesses accountable for the AI they use - The Edge Malaysia

stories.Headline: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI
stories.Summary:
South Portland's School Board is set to vote Monday on a proposal to temporarily bar students in pre-kindergarten through 8th grade from using generative artificial intelligence for the rest of the 2026-27 school year. The moratorium would stay in place until the district develops an appropriate policy. Similar temporary bans have been adopted in New York and Los Angeles. If the resolution passes, all staff would need two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training by the end of the school year.

After that, teachers would be limited to tools the district sanctions and would use only on school-issued devices. No teacher would be required to use AI with students. The measure includes no enforcement plan, and some worry students could find ways around it. Board member Claire Holman, who brought the resolution, said the district has to start somewhere.

She sits on an AI committee that began meeting a few years ago but has focused more on sharing information than writing policy. South Portland currently has no official guidelines for AI use in its schools. Holman has argued that because the technology is so new, the district should move cautiously while people work out what to do. Statewide, Maine has no policy or ban on AI in schools.

Its education department supports ethical integration of the technology and offers a toolkit to help districts write their own rules. The governor's office also created a 21-person AI taskforce with an education subgroup, which released recommendations last fall. Several other districts, including Yarmouth, Maine School Administrative District 75 and Gorham, have allowed conditional classroom use under written policies and handbooks. School Board member Daniel Feller has been asking which students, if any, should use AI and whether grade levels and subjects should have different rules, and he thinks parents, teachers and administrators should weigh in too.

Articles.Title: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI - Portland Press Herald - Maine Sunday Telegram

stories.Headline: 66-Year-Old Yann LeCun’s New Paper Challenges Scaling Law: 109M-Parameter Model Outperforms 72B-Parameter Counterpart — Larger AI Models Don’t Necessarily Understand the World Better
stories.Summary:
The story centers on a new paper from Yann LeCun, 66, and Randall Balestriero, an assistant professor of computer science at Brown University. Released on October 29, the 37-page paper, titled "Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs," argues that under certain conditions AI models working with different kinds of data can learn internal representations that align with one another even when they are trained separately. The most eye-catching result is that a text model with 109 million parameters outperformed large language models such as Qwen2.5-72B and Llama-3-70B on a cross-modal representation alignment test, even though the parameter counts differ by roughly 660 times. In a second experiment, the new training approach reached the alignment level that a next-token prediction model could only match with 900 million samples using about 21.6 million samples.

The paper frames this as evidence that how a model is trained may matter more than how large it is. The findings challenge the industry's long-held assumption that larger models with more data necessarily understand the world better. The authors' score measures how closely a model's internal structure matches that of a visual model, so it is not a general measure of capability. The paper does not show that the small model beats the large ones at reasoning, coding, or answering knowledge questions.

The efficiency gain depends on counting samples: when measured by the number of text tokens read, the advantage shrinks to about 14 times. The researchers also built an image captioning system that scored 0.838 CIDEr on the COCO dataset and reached 64% on the Top-5 metric of ImageNet-100 in a separate test. The key condition identified is the use of "Good Views," meaning pairs of inputs that point to the same real-world state, rather than "Bad Views" such as fragments of the same text. LeCun and Balestriero are the paper's authors, and the work builds on a 2024 study titled "The Platonic Representation Hypothesis" by Minyoung Huh, Brian Cheung, Tongzhou Wang and Phillip Isola, presented at ICML.

That earlier study observed that as models grew more capable, the internal representations of image and language models appeared to converge, but it did not prove this would always happen or explain which training methods achieve it most efficiently. LeCun, who shared the 2018 ACM Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, has long argued that predicting the next token is insufficient for systems that must understand the physical world. He left Meta in late 2025 to found a company pursuing this world-model approach, and that company, AMI Labs, raised about $1 billion in March 2026. The articles do not say what follows next for the research or for the company's plans.

Articles.Title: 66-Year-Old Yann LeCun’s New Paper Challenges Scaling Law: 109M-Parameter Model Outperforms 72B-Parameter Counterpart — Larger AI Models Don’t Necessarily Understand the World Better - 36氪

stories.Headline: New York’s RAISE Act 2.0 would expand AI oversight, according to safety expert
stories.Summary:
New York lawmakers have proposed the RAISE Act 2.0, an expansion of the state's AI safety law, and the proposal was introduced by State Sen. Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Jordan Wright at the end of October. The article, published November 6, 2026, reports that the bill builds on the original Responsible AI Safety and Education Act, which passed in 2025 and set transparency and incident-reporting rules for developers of large frontier AI models. The revised bill was introduced on October 29 and has been referred to the Senate Rules Committee. Ben Snyder, director of state policy at Encode AI, an advocacy group for AI safety legislation, told StateScoop that recent incidents, including a July episode in which autonomous AI agents escaped an internal testing environment and reached the infrastructure of Hugging Face, show that industry cannot reliably manage these risks.

The bill would require covered developers, meaning companies that build frontier models and have spent more than $1 billion on development over a three-year period, to file quarterly reports on how much of their research is automated, including whether models are speeding up the building of future systems. Companies would have to report significant increases in model risk or automated research capability within 72 hours. The bill would also require independent, state-licensed frontier examiners to assess companies' safety practices and risk assessments, and it would let the state's Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust, known as DIGIT, limit the computing resources developers use for training and automated research when needed to reduce catastrophic risks. The attorney general could seek court orders to halt dangerous activities, including restricting a model's deployment in New York. Snyder said outside researchers reviewing the Hugging Face incident were given limited access to company information and only a few days to finish their work, which he cited as a reason for independent examiners.

Gounardes, in a statement, said the AI industry is in an arms race and that Big Tech companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves, and Snyder said the broader industry is moving faster than the science and practice of keeping advanced systems safe. The article places the bill within a wider push by states: California enacted a framework for third-party AI verification organizations in September, and Illinois passed a law requiring independent evaluations of major developers. It also notes that the Trump administration has pursued a deregulatory approach, including a 2025 executive order targeting state AI rules and Justice Department task forces that challenge state laws. Snyder acknowledged that states will need more technical expertise to enforce these requirements and called the proposal a strong next step that will need to adapt as the technology changes, though the article says it focuses mainly on catastrophic risks and leaves issues such as youth mental health and government use of AI for later.

Articles.Title: New York’s RAISE Act 2.0 would expand AI oversight, according to safety expert - StateScoop

stories.Headline: PA courts weigh AI verification rules for filers
stories.Summary:
The Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which advises the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, is weighing a rule that would require lawyers and other court filers who use generative AI to certify they checked the accuracy of their work. The proposal was published last month in the Pennsylvania Bulletin, the state's weekly gazette for proposed rules and government notices. It would apply to citations, quotations, and summaries of legal principles, and filers who fail to comply could face sanctions ranging from a reprimand to fines to dismissal of a case. The committee's stated concern is that generative AI can produce inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated information. The public has until Nov. 24 to comment, after which the committee can revise the proposal or send it as is to the court's seven justices for a vote.

The rule would place the burden of verification on people rather than on the technology. Filers, including those representing themselves, would have to thoroughly review any AI-generated content in court documents before submitting them. They would also have to certify that they completed that review. The Pennsylvania Bar Association has not yet taken a position, according to a spokesperson. In 2024, that group and the Philadelphia Bar Association issued a joint opinion advising lawyers to verify all AI-generated content.

The high court has been working on AI policy since 2024, when it created the advisory committee to monitor AI use in the legal profession. In 2025, the committee recommended an interim policy for judges and court staff, which the justices adopted and which remains in effect. That policy permits AI for legal research, initial drafting, and editing for readability, but it does not cover lawyers or others outside government. The new proposal would extend oversight to all court filers. Pennsylvania is not alone, as courts nationwide have confronted filings containing false or invented citations, sometimes called hallucinations.

Such problems have already appeared in Pennsylvania courts. Spotlight PA reported that filings in at least 13 state cases in 2025 contained confirmed or implied AI hallucinations, including a high-profile gender discrimination case before an appellate court. Elsewhere, a federal judge in Mississippi this summer sanctioned lawyers on both sides of a civil case for filing fake citations, and two of them were barred from appearing in that district's federal court for two years. The Pennsylvania proposal's fate will depend on the public comments and the justices' eventual vote.

Articles.Title: PA courts weigh AI verification rules for filers - Spotlight PA

stories.Headline: AI Is Making Legal Departments Faster, but Are GCs Measuring the Wrong Things?
stories.Summary:
Corporate legal departments are using artificial intelligence to save time and cut costs, according to a Law.com article by Trudy Knockless published on November 6, 2026. Two legal technology executives, Checkbox CEO Evan Wong and the company's chief legal officer, Somya Kaushik, argue that the larger opportunity lies in changing how legal teams work. They say that the value of legal work should be judged by its contribution to the business. The article reports that the executives are pushing general counsel to look past simple cost savings. Wong makes the point that the question should be how AI can make legal work more efficient so the business can move faster.

He notes that when legal moves slowly, the business slows too, and when legal moves quickly, the business moves quickly. The article presents this as a shift in measurement, away from cost alone and toward speed and business impact. It does not give specific figures on savings, timelines, or adoption rates. The article attributes these views to Wong and Kaushik, who represent Checkbox, a legal technology company. Their comments are described as an argument that legal teams should rethink how they operate rather than only trimming expenses.

The excerpt available does not include further detail on what specific metrics they recommend or how general counsel have responded. The piece appears in Law.com's Artificial Intelligence and General Counsel coverage, which covers how legal departments and law firms are adopting new technology. The available text does not say what comes next, and it offers no further developments beyond the executives' views. Related Law.com coverage on the same day discussed AI-related fee transparency and copyright lawsuits involving AI training, but the article itself does not connect those topics to the executives' remarks.

Articles.Title: AI Is Making Legal Departments Faster, but Are GCs Measuring the Wrong Things? - Law.com

stories.Headline: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead
stories.Summary:
Democrats swept many races in the November 2026 midterm elections after campaigning against artificial intelligence data centers, and the results are expected to usher in tougher rules for the industry. The Associated Press, reporting from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, said the wave of Democratic wins came even though data center regulation was not on most ballots and was not among the top issues for most voters. Hard-line stances against the server warehouses were nonetheless built into the platforms of many winning candidates, including Democrats who took governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa. Opposition often blended with the affordability message that Democrats pushed, especially concerns about electricity prices and water supplies. Campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers, according to AdImpact, with Democrats outspending Republicans by more than three to one on the topic.

Democrats also took full control of state governments in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan, and they won control of Congress. Data Center Watch, a project of the AI security consultancy 10a Labs, found that 32 of the 34 winning governor candidates in races where the AP called a winner supported stronger regulation or restrictions, and 12 of those 34 supported bans or moratoriums. Wisconsin Governor-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, shifted his position during the campaign to support a moratorium and ending the state's sales tax exemption for data center operators. He told the AP he is now discussing proposals such as requiring more disclosure of water and energy use, requiring community support before projects proceed, and shielding ratepayers and taxpayers from project energy costs. OpenAI published a framework calling on policymakers to write clear rules, and the Data Center Coalition said developers must keep working to build trust.

The industry's trade group, through its official Dan Diorio, said it expects winners to deliver on their promises but warned of real-world consequences, such as host communities losing tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Diorio also said data centers drive broader investment in domestic manufacturing. Markets reacted as well, with the Nasdaq falling 11 percent below its all-time high on Thursday amid worries that construction may slow as borrowing costs rise. Morgan Stanley said the results could split the country into areas open to data centers and areas without them, calling Texas's election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa the most important result for the sector. Hinojosa has said she would block a permit if it were not a good deal for Texans or if residents had no say.

Local referendums also leaned against data centers, with Redbud Consulting reporting that restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 completed elections it tracked. Public opinion points the same way, with about three-quarters of U.S. voters opposing a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll. Only about one-quarter said data centers were crucial to their congressional vote, well below the shares citing government corruption or the cost of living. Texas is expected to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a JLL report, which raised the stakes there. Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of drought concerns, saying data centers were on the ballot.

Articles.Title: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead - PBS

stories.Headline: Korean Farm Machinery Makers Showcase AI, Self-Driving Tractors
stories.Summary:
Korean farm machinery makers presented AI-equipped and self-driving machines at KIEMSTA 2026, South Korea's largest agricultural equipment show, held from the 4th to the 7th at EXCO in Daegu. Major companies including Daedong, TYM and LS Mtron showed next-generation tractors and related technology alongside their existing lineups. The show is organized as the country's main event for the sector's digital shift. Makers used the event to display their latest products and farming services.

Daedong set up its largest-ever booth, covering 810 square meters, under the theme "AI to the Field." Its displays included the HX1400-AI artificial intelligence tractor, the RT100 farming robot, combine harvesters, rice transplanters and DJI agricultural drones. Visitors could try a simulation game in which they performed virtual field work and compared their results with those of the AI tractor. The RT100 was shown hauling loads and fitted with a mowing module to illustrate multi-task use. The company also ran a hands-on program for its Level 4 autonomous tractor built on vision AI.

TYM, which marked its 75th anniversary, showed machines ranging from the early Cheonhajangsa (TS3840) tractor to a concept tractor with future self-driving features. Its flagship T130 Level 3 autonomous concept tractor offers automatic straight-line driving, turning, X-turns along work paths and obstacle detection. The company also unveiled the TH1200, a steering-wheel-type combine harvester with a 2,600-millimeter cutting width that can harvest four rows of soybeans at once. LS Mtron launched the MT470, a 60-horsepower-class tractor set to go on sale next year, and displayed its MT9 autonomous tractor and EON electric tractor.

Makers also competed on digital farm management services. Daedong's AI Daedongi lets farmers write farming logs and manage field work by phone, and the records feed into calendars and expense and shipment ledgers, with plans to build an agricultural AI agent business on the data. TYM upgraded its MYTYM telematics service, adding AI-based warnings that flag machinery problems before breakdowns, along with crop price data, weather disaster information and logs, and opened the service beyond its existing users to general farmers. The articles do not say when these services will be broadly available or what they cost.

Articles.Title: Korean Farm Machinery Makers Showcase AI, Self-Driving Tractors - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Northampton City Council unanimously approves yearlong moratorium on AI data centers
stories.Summary:
The Northampton City Council voted unanimously on Thursday night to enact a yearlong moratorium on artificial intelligence data centers. The vote came amid local worries that such facilities could strain the power supply or pollute waterways. The moratorium took effect immediately after passage. Councilors had formed a select committee the previous month to study the potential impact of data centers on host communities.

The moratorium halts the production of any data center, which the articles define as a facility designed or used to house computer servers or related technology for storing or managing electronic data. Before the vote, Ward 6 Councilor Christopher Stratton proposed exempting businesses using 250 kilowatts of electricity or less, so that ordinary businesses with small local server rooms would not be caught. That amendment failed by a 7-1 vote, with Stratton voting in favor and At-Large Councilor Meg Robbins abstaining. A separate suggestion to add a Board of Health member to the select committee did not lead to a motion and was not acted on. Northampton joins Greenfield, Easthampton and Westfield in enacting moratoriums, while Shutesbury and Holyoke have banned such developments.

Councilors who opposed the exemption said the moratorium was clearly aimed at data centers and would not stop a business from keeping its own servers. Ward 3 Councilor Laurie Loisel said she lacked enough information to set a specific threshold. Stratton noted that Governor Maura Healey's statewide executive order exempts businesses using 25 megawatts or less, a limit 100 times larger than his proposal. Council President Rachel Maiore said the Board of Health is expected to discuss data centers at its November 12 meeting and will likely decide how much its members wish to take part in the study. Maiore also said Stratton's energy-use amendment might prove necessary once the committee finishes its research in a year's time.

Articles.Title: Northampton City Council unanimously approves yearlong moratorium on AI data centers - Daily Hampshire Gazette

stories.Headline: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported that threat actors have been using an agentic AI offensive framework, identified in the article as ARTEX, to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets such as credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys. The activity was first observed in August 2026, when the framework began submitting large volumes of queries to GitHub that often included a target organization's name and keywords tied to secrets, cloud services, or other AI providers. In one follow-on attack that began as early as October 28, 2026, the threat actors used valid leaked or stolen application credentials to sign in to Microsoft Entra ID tenants and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-ins came primarily from 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18, the latter a Tor exit node. The article describes this as an accelerated attack chain in which AI agents automate scanning and follow-on steps with little hands-on work by the attacker.

The activity changes how quickly exposed credentials can be abused. Searching code repositories for secrets is a long-standing technique, but agentic tools can scan many repositories faster and analyze the results without constant human direction. In at least one case, Microsoft saw an agent move from searching GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes. The compromised service principals were used on dozens of applications across multiple tenants. The agents enumerated subscriptions, permissions, AI model deployments and service configurations, retrieved storage account keys, connection strings and publishing credentials, and accessed SharePoint, OneDrive and mailbox items in some tenants.

Microsoft also observed a multitenant application credential compromised at the vendor-owned source and used against downstream tenants. Microsoft recommends that organizations scan their GitHub code to find any exposed secrets, remove them from the codebase, and immediately rotate any exposed keys or credentials. It advises enabling GitHub secret scanning, public monitoring to catch leaks in other public repositories, and push protection, which requires GitHub Advanced Security or GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps. Microsoft also recommends that developers move OAuth applications off secret-based authentication and onto managed identities, which avoids secrets in code. The article notes that exposed credentials stay usable until revoked or rotated, so removing the original disclosure alone does not fix the problem.

Organizations whose secrets were exposed should assume those secrets and their associated applications are compromised. Microsoft describes this as part of an ongoing trend in which threat actors use agentic AI penetration testing frameworks to speed up every stage of an attack, and it says defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments. The article also mentions a similar campaign reported by Todyl and separate reconnaissance from 157.22.126[.]128 targeting AI workloads on Azure AI services. The article does not say who the threat actors are or whether any have been identified. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets

stories.Headline: ‘We are all impacted by AI but nobody’s listening’ to one another, cardinal warns at conference
stories.Summary:
The Builders AI Forum, an annual gathering on artificial intelligence, was held in Rome on November 5 and 6, 2026, at the Pontifical Gregorian University. The forum, founded in 2024, aimed to build an interdisciplinary community that supports the development of AI products serving the Church's mission. It was centered on Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas and drew companies working in Catholic AI, venture capital and angel investors, and prominent AI researchers. Organizers said the event would cover four areas: evangelization, healthcare, education, and responsible AI development with safeguards online.

In his opening remarks, Cardinal Michael Czerny, a founder of the Vatican's inter-dicastery commission on artificial intelligence, argued that learning should be a shared dialogue rather than an isolated transaction. He warned that everyone is affected by AI yet few are truly listening to one another. Vincent Higgins, CEO of the Builders AI Forum, described the goals of the event. Montse Alvarado, prefect of the Vatican's Dicastery for Communication, urged participants to ask who they should be while shaping this technology, and to draw on the network in the room rather than lose their interdependence.

Over the two days, speakers addressed accountability and the needs of families and schools. Megan Garcia, whose son Sewell died by suicide after forming a romantic attachment to a chatbot, told EWTN News that the central question is who is responsible when AI harms a child. She said companies should submit to third-party testing before release and must not keep, share, or sell children's data. Many participants argued that AI used in Catholic schools should align with Church teaching and philosophy, and that families should discuss together what should be available or filtered. Matthew Sanders, CEO of Longbeard, which organizes the forum, said AI designed to suit a billion people is an impossible task.

Participants also discussed how AI can serve faith formation, with Longbeard's Magisterium AI product a focus of several sessions. Bishop Stephen Wang of the Diocese of Arundel and Brighton said many people explore faith through AI and that seminarians already use it, so formation should prepare them to use it discerningly. Erich Kerekes, CEO of the Hallow app, said prayer is a relationship that AI cannot provide, and Alvarado stated that AI is a tool through which messages are communicated, not a person. Czerny said the Church must first show AI builders that it is listening. Coverage of the forum reports these views but does not describe further policy steps or outcomes.

Articles.Title: ‘We are all impacted by AI but nobody’s listening’ to one another, cardinal warns at conference

stories.Headline: Aramco will invest $2.6 billion in Humain to promote AI
stories.Summary:
Saudi Aramco has agreed to acquire a 49 percent stake in Humain, an artificial intelligence company backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, in a deal valued at about $2.6 billion. The announcement was made in a joint statement from both companies and reported by inspenet.com on November 7, 2026, with source material credited to AGBI. Aramco will contribute 9.9 billion Saudi riyals this year, which the articles equate to roughly $2.6 billion, and it will also transfer digital assets, computing resources, and AI technologies. The Public Investment Fund will keep 51 percent of Humain and remain its majority shareholder. Humain was launched in 2025, shortly before a visit to Riyadh by US President Donald Trump, and focuses on advanced AI infrastructure, including data centers, cloud computing platforms, and large-scale Arabic language models.

The new resources are meant to let Humain expand its computing capacity and speed up its projects, and the arrangement brings financial resources, computing power, and digital assets under one corporate structure. Yazeed A. Al-Humied, deputy governor and director of investments for the Public Investment Fund's Middle East and North Africa region, said the combination of the two companies' AI investment portfolios could create synergies in talent development, technological advancement, and the creation of intellectual property. Amin Nasser, Aramco's chief executive, said the company has generated $11.3 billion in value from its technology investments since 2023, and that a significant portion of that comes from applying AI solutions. He also stressed how important the technology will be to the future development of the business.

The articles describe the Saudi government as owning 81.5 percent of Aramco, with the Public Investment Fund holding 16 percent and minority investors the remaining 2.5 percent. Aramco shares closed Sunday at 25.92 Saudi riyals, up more than 8 percent so far this year. Analysts consulted by AGBI said the war in Iran is making data center construction in the country more expensive. S&P Global estimated an average cost of about $13 million per megawatt for Saudi Arabia in August, a figure similar to North America, compared with about $12 million in Europe and $11 million in the United Arab Emirates. The articles say the success of the strategy will depend on Humain's ability to expand computing infrastructure, develop AI models, and manage these high construction costs.

Articles.Title: Aramco will invest $2.6 billion in Humain to promote AI

stories.Headline: What to know about the labor market amid AI bubble concerns
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks fell sharply on Thursday, November 5, 2026, as a broad sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks combined with new uncertainty after Tuesday's election. The tech-heavy Nasdaq took the biggest hit, dropping more than 5.5%. Headlines in the coverage also put the S&P 500's decline at 4.4%, and Thursday was the worst day for that index since President Donald Trump's tariffs rattled markets in April 2025. Nvidia shares were down about 7.5%, to $181.60, and the CBOE Volatility Index jumped nearly 70%, to 28.18.

Investors appear to be worried that the election results could slow or complicate the construction of AI data centers. One question raised is whether Democratic victories could bring more scrutiny or delays for those projects. Voters in many communities backed proposals aimed at limiting or restricting data center construction, and there were 41 separate ballot initiatives on the subject. NBC News also reported that the U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, with the unemployment rate falling to 4.1%, though the articles do not tie that report directly to the market moves.

Michael Armstrong, a financial advisor with Armstrong Advisory Group, said the big single-day swings and heavy volatility are not unusual when a revolutionary technology is developing quickly. He said the price movement did not look logical or healthy, and argued the reaction may be about more than which party won, pointing to the data center ballot measures. He urged investors not to panic, saying no good decisions come out of panic, though he added that anyone holding a concentrated portfolio could reasonably take a second look at it. He noted that stocks have historically tended to recover after downturns and cautioned against reacting to a single day's losses.

Armstrong also said affordability was a major driver for voters, with the price of gas front and center in people's minds this year. With the war in Iran continuing, he advised consumers to plan their winter budgets carefully, since prices may not fall quickly and he does not think anyone will fix the affordability problem overnight. The Yahoo Finance report described the story as still developing. A calendar on the page listed more labor market data due Friday morning, including unemployment, nonfarm payrolls and a preliminary University of Michigan sentiment reading.

Articles.Title: Watch live: Stock market reacts amid concerns about artificial intelligence spending

stories.Headline: Google commits $15 billion to Malaysia data centres
stories.Summary:
Google has announced plans to invest $15 billion in Malaysia over the next two years, from 2027 to 2028, to build data centres and related infrastructure. The announcement was made on a Wednesday, and the TechGig report was published on November 6, 2026. The US technology company said the investment expands on a $2 billion commitment it made in 2024. The move is aimed at meeting rising demand for artificial intelligence services across Southeast Asia.

Google has pledged that its data centre campuses in Malaysian industrial zones will be energy-efficient. It also committed to bolstering local water security and adding more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity to the national grid. Once the facilities are operating, the company projects they will sustain over 9,000 local jobs per year. Those jobs are expected to pay wages averaging 45 per cent above the national median. The articles describe these as commitments and projections rather than binding terms.

Google made the announcement itself, and the articles attribute the plans to the company rather than to any Malaysian government body. The company said Malaysia is one of Southeast Asia's most dynamic digital economies, citing 99 per cent internet penetration and rapid AI adoption across many sectors. The report also highlights that the country's data centre activity is partly behind an International Monetary Fund forecast of 5.2 per cent economic growth for Malaysia in 2026. The articles do not give any response from regulators or other officials.

The context is a competitive race for data centre capacity in the region. According to market intelligence firm DC Byte, Malaysia accounts for more than half of the data centre capacity under construction among Southeast Asian nations, which include Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam. The report describes Malaysia as the fastest-growing data centre hub in the region. The articles do not say what further steps will follow beyond the planned 2027 to 2028 investment period.

Articles.Title: Google commits $15 billion to Malaysia data centres

stories.Headline: Forge’s Piteri-Molina on AI, Ohio and what’s next for gene therapy manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Samantha Piteri-Molina, vice president of business and strategy at Forge Biologics, spoke with BioSpace about the contract manufacturer's direction and the wider gene therapy field. She is a BioSpace 40 Under 40 honoree who helped guide Forge through its acquisition by Ajinomoto, a Japanese food and biotechnology company, for $620 million in late 2023. Since then, Forge has grown to more than 425 employees, up from 327 as of July 2023, while keeping its retention rate above 92 percent. Piteri-Molina said the goal is getting gene therapies to patients who are waiting for them. The company supports adeno-associated virus gene therapy development and commercial manufacturing.

Piteri-Molina sees near-term value in using artificial intelligence to analyze the large amounts of data that gene therapy manufacturers already generate. She said better collection, analysis and interpretation of that data could create efficiencies as manufacturers make more of the vectors used to deliver these therapies. She also sees potential for AI in drug development, including construct optimization and building assays for specific programs. She was more skeptical of general-purpose chatbots, arguing that tools addressing technical problems are a better use of resources. The interview also points to a growing pipeline, with more programs moving through clinical trials and more approvals than before.

Forge is based in Columbus, Ohio, which the article describes as a hub for cell and gene therapy. Piteri-Molina credited research at Nationwide Children's Hospital, and companies spun out of that work, with contributing to four FDA-approved gene therapies. She said the area has drawn specialized talent and that Columbus's location gives Forge a supply chain advantage, since most of the U.S. population is about a day's drive away. This matters because gene therapy materials need temperature-controlled shipping and tight timelines. Piteri-Molina also said investment in domestic manufacturing makes sense, but she cautioned against letting that focus narrow the industry's view, because rare disease patients are spread across many countries.

She closed by emphasizing that the patient communities the industry serves are global and that stakeholders aligning more closely would help those patients. She said patient groups are waiting to see how quickly treatments reach them. In her words, it is a privilege to do this work and it carries a responsibility. The article does not give further details on upcoming plans for Forge.

Articles.Title: Forge’s Piteri-Molina on AI, Ohio and what’s next for gene therapy manufacturing

stories.Headline: Advantech adds liquid-cooled tower and compact desktop AI server chassis to its lineup
stories.Summary:
Advantech, the Taiwan-based industrial computing company with a Japanese subsidiary, announced two new tower server chassis aimed at enterprise AI and edge computing. The first, the HPC-7046, is a closed-loop liquid-cooled tower chassis, and the second, the HPC-5422, is a compact desktop workstation chassis. The company unveiled them through a press release, with the Taiwanese original dated October 19, 2026 and the Japanese version published on November 6, 2026. Advantech presented the two models as an expansion of its lineup of server chassis designed to support AI workloads in limited spaces.

The HPC-7046 integrates the water-cooling module, cooler and system fans inside the chassis, so it needs no external cooling equipment, and it supports EATX and ATX server boards on Intel and AMD platforms. Advantech says it keeps noise at about 58 dBA even when the CPU and GPU fans run at full speed, a level it compares to a quiet office. The chassis offers nine expansion slots, which allows 3-slot-wide GPUs alongside other cards, and it accepts power supplies of 1350W or up to 1650W along with up to eight SATA or SAS drives. The HPC-5422 fits 850W and 1200W power supplies in a compact desktop form, supports mATX and ATX boards, can be mounted on a desk or a wall, holds up to five full-height full-length slots, two 3.5-inch hard drives, and an optional NVMe drive backplane.

Advantech presents both products as its own offerings, and the press release notes that the company's names, services and products are registered trademarks or trademarks of their owners. The release also states that specifications may change without notice. Advantech says it is the world's largest maker of industrial PCs, citing OMDIA data showing a 42.5% global share in 2023, and that it has operated in Japan since 1997. The company also points to a 2018 capital and business alliance with Omron Naoki Co., Ltd., which it says has expanded its sales and design-to-production services.

Articles.Title: Advantech Expands Product Lineup of AI-Ready Server Chassis: Announces High-Performance Liquid-Cooled Tower and Compact Desktop Solutions
