IREN jumped roughly 20% in a single session after releasing its first quarter 2027 results, a sharp turnaround for a stock that had fallen more than 40% over the prior month. Investors responded most strongly to the company's artificial intelligence cloud business, which generated about US$200 million of the US$228 million in total revenue. Adjusted EBITDA margin came in near 29%, a notable step up from roughly 14% in the prior quarter. The results point to a shift away from legacy bitcoin mining toward AI infrastructure services.

Total revenue fell from US$240 million a year earlier, but the mix moved decisively toward AI cloud. The company still reported a net loss of US$263 million, compared with net income of US$385 million a year earlier, and a loss of US$0.66 per share. Management described its AI capacity for 2026 as largely sold out and said discussions for 2027 and 2028 were advanced. Its Horizon 1 facility is live with Microsoft, and operating annual recurring revenue reached US$1.0 billion.

The company, however, pushed its US$4 billion ARR target into early 2027 rather than late 2026, and it still plans a fiscal 2027 capital spending program of US$25 billion to US$30 billion funded largely with debt and customer prepayments. Bulls see the quarter as evidence that IREN is becoming a contracted AI utility, while bears worry that rising overhead, interest costs and the decommissioning of mining hardware will run ahead of recognized AI revenue. The timing of new capacity coming online late in the quarter is central to that concern. The articles indicate that the coming quarters will show whether the company can convert its contracted backlog into revenue while financing a very large build-out.

Articles.Title: IREN (IREN) Stock Price Rallies As Q1 Results Spotlight AI Margins

stories.Headline: AI’s Hidden Footprint, From Quartz Mines to Kenyan Click-Workers, Bared in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Doc ‘The Technological Sublime’
stories.Summary:
A documentary titled "The Technological Sublime," directed by Jannes Callens, is heading to the Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei, where it will be shown as a work in progress. The film follows the physical supply chain that keeps artificial intelligence running, beginning at quartz mines in the Appalachians and moving on to chip plants in Taiwan, lithium fields in Chile, undersea cables and click-workers in Kenya. Its aim is to show what the technology costs people and the planet. The festival runs from November 6 to 9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency. Callens says that AI is often discussed as something abstract and invisible, but his research showed a tangible ecosystem behind the idea of "green" AI.

He noted that an online image search for AI mostly returns humanlike robots, with almost nothing showing the hardware and labor underneath, which pushed him toward the subject. He describes the film as a work of art meant to bring nuance to the AI debate by showing the achievements of the technology without ignoring its material, ecological and human costs. His earlier documentary, "Dor (Longing)," won the Best Belgian Film award at the Brussels Independent Film Festival and was selected for Visions du Réel. The first scenes of the new film have already been shot, and the team is waiting to secure the rest of its financing.

Delegate producer Steven Dhoedt, who has long followed new technology, said many people still find AI abstract despite the hype around it. He praised Callens for choosing a grounded, less sensational approach, which he believes suits the moment. Because filming spans four continents, the producers are still seeking more investors and partners. Belgian broadcaster VRT has come on board, and talks are underway with other European broadcasters.

The team is also working with James Chia-Hao Hsu of Reel Asia Pictures, its Taiwan partner, to start conversations with distributors and sales agents at the festival. The film is a co-production between Brussels-based Visualantics, Paris-based Tag Film, Cobra Films and Taipei-based Reel Asia Pictures. Dhoedt said TCCF gives the project a real chance to reach audiences in Asia. The article does not say when the finished film will be released or whether it has secured a distributor.

Articles.Title: AI’s Hidden Footprint, From Quartz Mines to Kenyan Click-Workers, Bared in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Doc ‘The Technological Sublime’

stories.Headline: SK Hynix (KOSE:A000660) Unveils Cooler AI Memory As Data Center Scrutiny Grows
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, listed in Seoul as KOSE:A000660, introduced an iHBM low-heat memory design that it says is meant to reduce cooling demands in AI data centers. The company presented the new iHBM architecture as offering lower power use and less heat output than conventional high bandwidth memory used in AI servers. The announcement was reported on November 6, 2026, with the article published that day. Management framed the product as a response to growing scrutiny of the water and electricity consumed by data centers running AI workloads.

According to the report, the launch is also part of a broader effort to attract and retain chip engineers as Chinese competitors expand their hiring. The article describes SK hynix as a global memory and semiconductor supplier that makes chips for data centers, consumer devices and enterprise hardware. Any shift in its product mix toward lower power iHBM would therefore affect how AI infrastructure is built and cooled. The report does not give pricing, shipment dates or specific figures on power or heat savings.

The article is an AI-assisted analysis produced by Simply Wall St. and carried by Yahoo Finance, and it does not name a company official as a direct speaker. It states that management positioned iHBM as a response to scrutiny of data center water and electricity use, and that SK hynix highlighted the launch in connection with talent retention. The piece also says the company's long-term success depends on continued heavy capacity expansion, including new fabs and advanced packaging, while keeping its balance sheet disciplined. It stresses that it is general commentary and not investment advice.

The article presents the iHBM launch as a test of the bull case for SK hynix's heavy AI memory investment, since it targets power and cooling pressures in AI servers. It also notes the bear case that a custom low-heat design adds technical complexity and capital needs at a time when Chinese DRAM rivals are raising pay to recruit engineers. The report says nothing firm about what happens next beyond these competing considerations. It is also unclear from the article whether the iHBM design has begun commercial shipments.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix (KOSE:A000660) Unveils Cooler AI Memory As Data Center Scrutiny Grows

stories.Headline: Review Links 5G, 6G, and AI for Maize Disease Monitoring
stories.Summary:
A systematic review published in Discover Networks evaluates 62 research papers on intelligent wireless sensing systems built for AI-enabled maize disease monitoring. The authors, Kayombo Sakachiva, Jackson Phiri, and Mayumbo Nyirenda, drew on literature from January 2019 to 2026 to assess how 5G and emerging 6G technologies can support real-time crop health analysis. Their work points to a move away from manual field inspections toward automated, data-driven precision agriculture, especially in resource-limited rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa. The reviewed systems combine multi-modal sensing, edge intelligence, and unmanned aerial vehicles to spot disease before symptoms show, which matters because maize pathogens can cut yields by 40% to 90%.

The review ties its focus to food security, noting that the global population is projected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050. In Zambia, maize covers more than 65% of farmland and supports over 60% of the population, so the stakes are high there. The authors say traditional monitoring is labor-intensive and error-prone, while AI-based detection can automate the work and reduce labor needs. The synthesis frames this shift as part of "Agriculture 4.0," which brings together computer vision, deep learning, and Internet of Things tools. The authors followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and searched IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, starting from 152 results and keeping 62 studies.

The authors report that AI-based edge computing paired with multi-modal fusion is especially promising. Hybrid models such as CNN-LSTM networks reached detection accuracies of 96% to 97% in early-stage maize disease detection, according to the review. Non-visual sensors, including volatile organic compound detectors and ultrasound probes, can pick up plant stress before visible lesions form, though they have limits. The review notes that VOC sensors can take seconds to minutes to respond because of gas diffusion, and ultrasound penetrates dense foliage poorly. On the network side, Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication in 5G targets end-to-end latency below 10 milliseconds, while 6G is projected to reach 0.01 to 0.1 milliseconds.

The review also covers non-terrestrial networks, unmanned aerial vehicles, federated learning, and energy use, all of which bear on remote farms. Satellites and high-altitude platforms could extend connectivity to off-grid fields, and drones could extend monitoring range despite battery and Doppler challenges. Federated learning would let models train across devices without pooling farm data, which could protect smallholder privacy. The authors say edge processing can cut transmission energy use by 30% to 60%, and they name energy harvesting and lightweight AI as ways to extend sensor life. The review also lists persistent gaps, including few large-scale tropical field trials, interoperability problems, high costs for smallholders, and signal losses of 10 to 30 dB in dense maize.

The authors call for realistic propagation models, hybrid edge-cloud designs, and collaboration among technology developers, agricultural extension agencies, and regulators to move these systems into practice. The review finds research interest peaked between 2023 and 2025 but says crop-specific maize work in tropical conditions remains underexplored. Its authors describe the work as a foundation for future empirical studies on scalable and privacy-aware sensing systems. The articles do not describe any deployment timeline or planned field programs.

Articles.Title: Review Links 5G, 6G, and AI for Maize Disease Monitoring

stories.Headline: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Just Issued a 6-Word Warning That Could Spell Disaster for AI Stocks
stories.Summary:
On October 28, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said "Interest rates get in the cracks," and added that rates affect almost everything, including the AI data center buildout that is largely financed with borrowed money. In the month ending November 6, CoreWeave fell 47.54% and Nebius dropped 45.4%, while Microsoft edged up 0.16%. The market has begun to sort AI companies by whether they pay for data centers with cash or borrow to build them. The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point in September and held it at 3.75% to 4.00% in October. As of November 3, CME FedWatch put the odds of another December hike at 72%.

Long-term rates add more pressure. The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.24% on October 9 and stood at 4.84% on November 5, the same day the VIX rose to 28.18, its highest reading since early August. CoreWeave has a revenue backlog of $104.2 billion but plans $35 billion to $39 billion in capital spending this year, and its debt is 8.94 times its equity. Its second-quarter interest expense was $640 million, up from $267 million a year earlier, and management expects $860 million to $940 million in the third quarter. Nebius plans $20 billion to $25 billion of capital spending this year, backed by $37.5 billion in signed future revenue, and three customers made up 24%, 21% and 14% of its second-quarter revenue.

Oracle holds $664 billion in signed future revenue but spent $28.5 billion on capital projects last quarter and burned $5.4 billion in free cash flow, with interest expense up 55%. When asked when free cash flow would turn positive, CFO Hilary Maxson said the company has not given a timeframe. Microsoft produced $18.6 billion of free cash flow last quarter after $45.2 billion in capital spending, and CFO Amy Hood said it has not yet borrowed in the debt markets. Alphabet, by contrast, had negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion and raised $28.7 billion from new bonds. Micron generated $62.3 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2026, yet its stock fell 36.57% over the past month, because its memory orders come from companies that borrow to build.

The article points to two near-term tests. CoreWeave's third-quarter earnings report will show whether interest expense reaches the top of its guidance or whether the company cuts its spending plan. The Fed's December meeting follows, and a rate hike would raise financing costs on contracts priced when money was cheaper. Demand for AI has held up so far, but the open question is whether the borrowing behind the expansion still pays off at today's rates.

Articles.Title: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Just Issued a 6-Word Warning That Could Spell Disaster for AI Stocks

stories.Headline: McDonald's will expand AI ordering to save 50 hours of labor weekly. Franchisees question the costs
stories.Summary:
McDonald's plans to expand its AI ordering system, Archy, to additional drive-thrus in the United States and Australia, according to Restaurant Dive. The company hopes the technology will save about 50 labor hours a week at its restaurants. CEO Chris Kempczinski announced the expansion during an earnings call, where he also said more overseas trials are scheduled for 2027. Most U.S. McDonald's restaurants are expected to receive the system, which takes voice orders in both Spanish and English.

The labor savings form part of a wider technology initiative that the company says is meant to raise restaurant margins by 2.5 percentage points. Archy sits alongside automated inventory tracking and connected equipment within the ArchIQ AI platform, which the chain announced in September as part of its Next initiative. During that September investor day, McDonald's reported that Archy's accuracy exceeded 90 percent and that customer satisfaction was high in early tests. Kempczinski said the technology would let staff focus on customer service and food quality, and he promised updates on Next throughout 2027.

Franchisees have raised doubts about whether the benefits will outweigh the costs. According to Peter Saleh, an analyst who covers restaurants and food distributors, operators said in October that the margin target seemed highly theoretical and that few details had been given about how productivity would improve. Saleh wrote that franchisees were most enthusiastic about the inventory management tools, which some believe could cut manager hours and food waste. Operators also questioned whether the consumer actually wants AI taking orders, and whether voice ordering fits with the company's renewed focus on service and hospitality.

The article places the expansion within a broader debate in the fast-food industry about automation and human service. Chick-fil-A has said its drive-thru orders will stay human-to-human even as rivals test AI, and McDonald's is retraining two million workers as chains reconsider kiosks and apps. The articles also note that AI systems depend on energy-hungry computing infrastructure that can strain resources and raise power bills. The articles do not say when the U.S. rollout will be complete, and they leave open how the costs will be split between the company and its franchisees.

Articles.Title: McDonald's will expand AI ordering to save 50 hours of labor weekly. Franchisees question the costs

stories.Headline: AMD: AI Panic Meets Outsized CPU/GPU Gains - Upgrade To Buy
stories.Summary:
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD) has remained volatile since an analyst's Hold rating in August 2026, according to a Seeking Alpha opinion piece published on November 7, 2026, as investor sentiment on AI swings between enterprise adoption of agentic AI and broader concerns. The author, who writes under the name Juxtaposed Ideas, argues that the stock has fallen more than 30% despite the company's strong position. The article reports that AMD is trading at a price-to-earnings ratio of 50.15 times. It says the same selloff has pushed the stock to a long-term target of $955.40, which the author sees as a possible doubling from current levels. The author also points to record shipments of AMD's EPYC server processors as evidence of growth.

The article's central claim is that AMD's gains in server processors should continue, with the author expecting further gains in x86 server market share. The author cites Intel's supply chain delays running through the second half of 2027 as a factor that may help AMD, and says AMD guided server revenue to double year over year in 2027. The piece notes that AMD is expanding its data center wins with existing and new customers, and that it works closely with AI foundry labs. These points are presented as supporting a robust and profitable growth outlook. The author therefore recommends an upgrade to a Buy rating.

The article is written by Juxtaposed Ideas, a full-time analyst with a Seeking Alpha following of about 16,350, and the author states a long position in AMD, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Broadcom. The author also says the piece reflects personal opinion and is not professional investment advice. Seeking Alpha adds its own disclaimer that past performance does not guarantee future results and that its contributors may not be licensed. The article also warns that AMD's volatility may persist because of its growing data center and AI exposure and a projected decline in PC market shipments in 2027. It advises investors to practice position sizing discipline.

Articles.Title: AMD: AI Panic Meets Outsized CPU/GPU Gains - Upgrade To Buy

stories.Headline: Hideo Kojima AI: Creativity Quotes, 5-10 Year View [2026]
stories.Summary:
Hideo Kojima, the creator of Metal Gear and DEATH STRANDING, has said that AI cannot replace the human act of making games and that the trend worries him. He made the case in an interview with the Japanese outlet Game*Spark, and English-language coverage followed, including a TechRadar report dated November 6 built around his view that the fun for creators lies in the creative process itself. The remarks were framed as a question of craft and enjoyment rather than only jobs or cost. Kojima did not name a specific AI tool, company, or product in the material reviewed.

Kojima acknowledged that AI can make development more efficient, so his argument is not that the technology is useless. His concern is that a workflow in which a creator tells a machine what to make, reviews the output, and asks for changes is not a form of creation he finds particularly interesting. He compared this to drawing, saying that getting a finished picture is not what makes drawing fun. He also said the trial and error in between is what gets his adrenaline pumping, and that he does not want a future where that part is lost. For him, the value sits in the process as well as the result.

Kojima made a hedged forecast in which he said he thinks things will be fine for the next five or 10 years. He then added a condition, saying that if AI continues unchecked, a future in which AI plays a vital role in creative fields may come someday. Coverage from GamesRadar carried a personal aside about not expecting to be around for that worst case, though the remark is best read as a worry about direction rather than a dated prediction. The word unchecked places the outcome in the hands of rules, norms, and creator choices.

Outlets framed the interview in different ways, with TechRadar stressing that AI cannot replace human creativity, AUTOMATON WEST focusing on the gap between efficiency and enjoyment, and GamesRadar emphasizing the personal angle. Kojima has previously described AI as a friend in some contexts, which makes this more measured stance part of a broader pattern rather than a flat rejection. Similar debates are unfolding across creative fields, and the interview adds a games-specific voice to that discussion. The articles do not report any studio plan, release date, or policy change tied to these remarks, so what follows remains open.

Articles.Title: Hideo Kojima AI: Creativity Quotes, 5-10 Year View [2026]

stories.Headline: Germany to Invest €50 Million in AI-Powered OSINT Intelligence
stories.Summary:
The German Armed Forces plan to spend €50 million on an IT tool that conducts open-source intelligence (OSINT) gathering from the internet using artificial intelligence. The report, published by militarnyi.com on 7 November 2026, cites the German publication Hartpunkt and its own sources. The purchase will be made through BWI GmbH, a company wholly owned by the federal government. The Bundestag's Budget Committee is set to review the proposal next week as part of the approval process for procurements valued above €25 million. The software, called Internet Reconnaissance, is intended to improve situational awareness and enhance troop safety.

Beyond analyzing text, the tool is designed to automatically analyze images and videos. Its stated purpose is to help commanders understand what is happening in the information environment around deployed forces. The articles do not describe the tool's technical architecture or its specific data sources. They also do not say whether the purchase has been approved.

The articles do not name the officials responsible for the procurement decision or quote any statement from the German government or the Bundeswehr about the tool. The proposal is described only through Hartpunkt's reporting and sources, and the articles do not indicate any official comment. Separately, the articles note that the German government has agreed to acquire 50% of the shares in the defense conglomerate KNDS from private owners, with the French government holding the remaining 50%. Once that deal is completed, KNDS will become a joint state-owned enterprise.

The articles present this as separate from the OSINT purchase. The article also lists other defense stories from the same feed, including reports on China's runway construction on Antelope Reef and Russia's expanded forced conscription of men. These items are not connected to the German procurement in the articles. The articles do not say what will happen next beyond the Budget Committee review.

Articles.Title: Germany to Invest €50 Million in AI-Powered OSINT Intelligence

stories.Headline: Apple at 36x Earnings Faces a $200 AI Cap [2026]
stories.Summary:
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) now trades at about 36 times forward earnings, a premium that has drawn attention alongside a report that the company is cutting the daily AI-tool budget for some of its engineers. Yahoo Finance quoted strategist Josh Brown calling Apple "the anti-AI large cap tech trade," a label that frames the stock's premium around a single question: whether Big Tech's heavy AI spending will pay off. The reports cited here describe the valuation and the spending changes as facts, while the claim that the premium rests on a shaky bet is an interpretation rather than a confirmed finding. Apple's forward multiple compares with a 10-year average of 24 times, and analysts reportedly expect only about 6% earnings-per-share growth in fiscal 2027. Moffett put the 36x level in yield terms at roughly 2.8%.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported that Apple lowered the daily AI-spending cap for some engineers from $300 to $200, a cut of one-third, and that further reductions could push some teams down to $100. The caps govern how much individual engineers spend on AI tools, not Apple's overall AI budget. Apple has not published a policy on these caps in the material cited, so the $100 level remains a possibility raised in the report. The reported financials show a split in spending, with capital expenditure down 28% to $6.8 billion over the first nine months of fiscal 2026 while research and development rose 33% to $34.0 billion. For the full fiscal year, R&D reached $45.8 billion, up 32%, with higher infrastructure and AI costs cited.

Bernstein analyst Mark Newman said Apple is not committing the roughly $100 billion-plus in annual AI capital expenditure that some peers spend, citing Apple capex of about $13 billion in the prior year and about $11 billion in the current year. Josh Brown read Apple as a hedge for investors who doubt that AI infrastructure spending will earn its keep, so that if AI capex disappoints, the stock looks prudent for sitting it out. Dan Ives took a more bullish view, saying "20% of the world" will reach AI through an Apple device and that the company has found a way to spend very little on AI. Ives argues that distribution, rather than building the largest model, is the asset Apple holds. The analysts disagree on whether restraint is defensive or an efficient route to the same prize.

The context matters for what comes next. The AI sell-off earlier in this period hit companies with heavy infrastructure bills, while Apple sits on the other side of that trade with far less data-center spending than its peers. A 36x multiple leaves little cushion if growth stays near 6%, and the reports say nothing about whether Apple's restrained approach will hold. The articles do not indicate a specific next event that will settle the debate, so the outcome remains open.

Articles.Title: Apple at 36x Earnings Faces a $200 AI Cap [2026]

stories.Headline: AI physics startup PSI says a system running a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a quantum computing question open since 2008 (PSI)
stories.Summary:
Physical Superintelligence (PSI), an AI physics startup, announced on November 6, 2026 that a research system developed in-house had proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a question in quantum computing open since 2008. The system ran on PSI's own infrastructure and used instances of a non-public Anthropic model. According to the company, the system produced a complete proof on the third day of the run, and the Lean proof assistant, which checks each step by computer, accepted it. The system then worked on related open problems and improved the result twice, with Lean accepting the final version.

The conjecture concerns whether quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones on random inputs, which lack the structure that powers speedups like Shor's algorithm from 1994. The articles describe the proof as showing that, if the conjecture holds, an ordinary computer can predict a quantum computer's answer to a yes-or-no question about a random string while reading far fewer bits than the quantum machine would need, so no exponential advantage exists unless the string has a rare pattern. The proof rests on a plan by Shachar Lovett and Jiapeng Zhang, in which one inequality had been left as a conjecture. The PSI team replaced that inequality with a new one proved in the manuscript, drawing on earlier work by David Reimer and several other researchers.

David Turturean, a Member of Technical Staff at PSI, led the work, developing the research system, scoping the problem and running it, and he is responsible for the correctness of the paper. Jim Halverson, an Advisor at PSI, audited the proof, and Phiala Shanahan, also an Advisor, commented on the Lean formalization. Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan of Stanford University had earlier, in August 2026, settled a special case of the conjecture, and they have since read the full proof, sent comments and are writing a shorter exposition for experts. They called the result a huge advance that resolves a decades-old conjecture. Earlier work had established weaker bounds or special cases only, and the articles say PSI's proof completes the full conjecture.

Articles.Title: AI physics startup PSI says a system running a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a quantum computing question open since 2008 (PSI)

stories.Headline: AI and Databases Streamline Rice Trait Ontology Curation
stories.Summary:
A research team has built a computer platform that uses artificial intelligence and linked databases to speed up the curation of the Rice Trait Ontology, a standardized vocabulary for agricultural traits in rice. The system, described in a brief report in the journal Genomics & Informatics, connects the Rice-Alterome database with the PubAnnotation platform. Its goal is to cut the time and labor that experts have traditionally spent reviewing scientific papers by hand. The authors are Ahmad, Liu, Kim, Yao, Larmande and Xia, and the article was published with a 2025 citation, while the news report on it appeared in November 2026. The work was reported by Bioengineer.org and Scienmag.

The platform relies on large language models, named as DeepSeek and KIMI, which are connected through application programming interfaces to extract and check trait information from the literature. To reduce the risk of these models producing false statements, they work within a controlled environment built from curated data in Rice-Alterome and PubAnnotation. Rice-Alterome contains more than 500,000 sentences describing relationships between genes and other named entities, each linked to PubMed identifiers. The dataset covers about 8,169 genes and carries annotated Gene Ontology and Trait Ontology terms. A web interface lets authenticated experts search terms, verify entries and add, merge, remove or keep ontology classes.

The researchers described two examples to show how the system works in practice. In the first, a new class called "Seedling-stage submergence tolerance" was added, with evidence drawn from Rice-Alterome, PubAnnotation and NCBI totaling more than 100 results, and it was placed under the parent trait "submergence tolerance." In the second, the system retrieved 39 sentences and associated genes supporting a merger of "submergence tolerance" and "flooding tolerance," which the study treats as synonyms, so that experts could consolidate the two terms. To test reliability, three domain experts independently classified sentences for about 20 traits, and the team calculated Fleiss' kappa. The kappa value was 0.719, with observed agreement at 0.8733 and expected agreement at 0.5490, which the authors read as substantial agreement beyond chance.

The authors, who include the corresponding researchers listed on the paper, say the system balances automation with human oversight and is built on a Python Django back-end and a React front-end. They plan to extend the framework to other crops, specifically wheat and maize, and to refine the language model retrieval and annotation methods for better accuracy. The report concludes that combining specialized databases with large language models can address the challenges of manual curation as biological data grows. The articles do not say when the extension to other crops will occur or whether the platform is available for general public use.

Articles.Title: AI and Databases Streamline Rice Trait Ontology Curation

stories.Headline: AI Tool of the Week: this Gemini feature brings textbooks into AI learning
stories.Summary:
Google has added a feature to its Gemini Notebook, formerly known as NotebookLM, that lets students ask questions based on textbooks drawn from a built-in catalogue. The feature was described in a Mint article published on November 7, 2026, and Google's October 29 post says students can now access hundreds of textbooks from providers in the US and India. Answers come with inline citations and direct links to the original passages, so a student can check where the information comes from. The textbooks are free to use through the Add sources and Textbooks options within a notebook.

The feature addresses a problem the article describes: students who ask a general chatbot about a chapter may get confident answers that do not match the book their teacher follows, and they cannot easily verify them. Instead of downloading PDFs of the right edition, a student can select a book from the catalogue and ask questions grounded in it. Gemini Notebook can also turn a chapter into study guides, practice quizzes and flashcards. The article notes that the catalogue includes S Chand Publishing alongside OpenStax and the Open Textbook Library. It also says eligible ebooks bought on Google Play Books can already be added as sources.

The article was written by Jaspreet Bindra and Anuj Magazine, co-founders of AI&Beyond, as part of Mint's weekly "AI Tool of the Week" feature. It was excerpted from Leslie D'Monte's weekly TechTalk newsletter. The authors state that their tool recommendations are independent and based on their internal testing, and that the creators did not influence them. The article does not describe any response from Google beyond its October 29 post. It also does not say whether the catalogue will expand beyond the current set of providers or how schools and teachers are expected to adopt the tool.

Articles.Title: AI Tool of the Week: this Gemini feature brings textbooks into AI learning

stories.Headline: AI advising the White House? Why the task requires people—especially young folks
stories.Summary:
Jason Furman, a former chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Barack Obama and now a Harvard professor, recently said that if he were running the CEA today he would, somewhat regretfully, use current AI systems instead of hiring 20 human economists. He said the chair's job would be safe. After pushback, including from former staff, he softened his position and called for an AI-intensive CEA with only a skeleton staff. Under that version, he would still largely replace junior staff, recent college graduates and graduate students, with AI.

Furman based his argument on what AI can already do, pointing to a website he built called Econvitals that offers data dashboards, blog posts, memos, briefings and research papers. The author argues he is focusing on tasks rather than the organization's mission. The CEA, created in 1946, is meant to give the president objective economic advice on domestic and international policy. The author says its most important role is to stop bad ideas, and that AI models tend not to challenge them the way people do. Staff economists, many on leave from universities or detailed from the Federal Reserve or cabinet agencies, have less to lose by dissenting than political appointees.

The author, a Bloomberg Opinion columnist and former Federal Reserve economist, recalls working with junior staff who were often the first to notice when something did not add up. He describes a project his CEA year began with a magazine article about Americans unable to cover a $400 emergency expense, a finding that came from a Fed survey. Economists could not initially answer the president's question, and the work was creative rather than mechanical. The author says AI could speed data work and provide extra checks, and could help revisit researchers' views or tailor the Economic Report of the President to new audiences.

The author concludes that the CEA will change with AI, and that it should. He agrees with Furman that juniors spending their days overseeing bots would be a poor use of taxpayer money and talent, but argues that this reflects a choice about job design rather than a fact about AI. The same tools could free junior staff from monotonous data pulls and formatting so they can make quality improvements and pursue questions no one can yet answer. In the author's words, the president deserves a better CEA, not a smaller one.

Articles.Title: AI advising the White House? Why the task requires people—especially young folks

stories.Headline: Nvidia is driving the AI boom. Good
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, the American chipmaker whose graphics-processing units power artificial intelligence, has become the world's most valuable company, worth $5.4trn, according to an Economist analysis published by Mint on November 5, 2026. Its demand is described as insatiable, and the firm is projected to generate $370bn in net income next year and possibly reach $1trn in sales by 2029. The company's share price is said to be 14 times what it was when ChatGPT was released in late 2022. Nvidia alone accounts for 8% of the S&P 500, and the article notes that it has produced about 15 cents of every dollar the American stock market has returned since 2023.

The article describes a web of financing that has drawn comparisons to the dotcom era. Through $1trn-worth of deals, Nvidia provides cash or guarantees so that data-centre landlords and AI labs can buy its chips, and some critics call it the "bank of AI." Morgan Stanley estimates its overall credit exposure at $200bn by the start of 2029, which could later reach $300bn or more. The article also notes that Nvidia's share of research and development spending has fallen from over a fifth of sales to less than a tenth, while non-Nvidia AI chips now hold 38% of the market, up from 26% in 2023. Nvidia still keeps about $99bn in cash and expects to generate roughly $200bn this year.

The article's author argues that the worries are mostly unjustified and that the risks would fall largely on Nvidia's shareholders. It presents Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive, as a leader who believes the main obstacle to AI is insufficient infrastructure rather than weak demand, and who has concluded that the markets will not supply capital at the necessary scale. The article also reports that Goldman Sachs, BlackRock and Blackstone joined Nvidia last month in a $500bn data-centre initiative. It adds that AI revenue, from Anthropic and other firms and the hyperscalers, may now be around $150bn a year, far short of the $2.5trn needed for AI capital spending. The article concludes that if the bets fail, the costs will be borne mainly by investors, and if they succeed, the AI era may arrive sooner.

Articles.Title: Nvidia is driving the AI boom. Good

stories.Headline: AI-driven attacks put telecom security on govt radar
stories.Summary:
The Department of Telecommunications has stepped up efforts to protect India's telecom infrastructure from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, including those powered by artificial intelligence. According to officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, the department has held several rounds of meetings with Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Reliance Jio and state-owned BSNL to strengthen network firewalls and other protective measures. The talks follow a series of advisories from the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warning about AI-enabled intrusions. The reporting, published on 6 November 2026, does not give a single date for the start of the meetings.

The department has mandated annual network security audits for telecom service providers, including vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. External network audits are required once every three years. DoT has also set up a telecom security operations centre to improve monitoring, situational awareness and coordination on cybersecurity. Separately, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India has proposed draft guidelines for the responsible use of AI in telecom networks, which call for risk-based classification of AI systems, human oversight, safety assessments and reporting of serious AI-related incidents to the regulator. Under the proposal, operators would remain accountable for AI systems they deploy, including those built or supplied by third parties.

A senior DoT official said the department is working with the operators and that the telcos are independently building security mechanisms, which the official described as robust. The official said the department has not seen any untoward incidents involving private operators or BSNL. The Cellular Operators Association of India had not responded to queries at the time of publication. CERT-In, in an advisory dated 15 October, flagged AI agents that gained unauthorised access to ICT assets of Indian organisations, and in a 4 November advisory it reported escalating AI-driven attacks on banking, financial services and insurance entities by a threat actor it calls Crafty Falcon.

The article places the Indian effort against wider global activity. It notes that Singapore disclosed in the previous year that all four of its major telecom operators had been targeted by a Chinese-linked group, and that Singapore announced further cybersecurity steps in March 2026. It also recalls the Salt Typhoon campaign that affected AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile in the United States, which came to light in 2024. The article does not say when the DoT's further talks with operators will conclude or when TRAI's draft framework will be finalised.

Articles.Title: AI-driven attacks put telecom security on govt radar

stories.Headline: Delhi HC orders takedown of AI-generated videos targeting CM Rekha Gupta
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, the Delhi High Court ordered the removal of several social media posts and videos published by the Aam Aadmi Party that allegedly depicted Chief Minister Rekha Gupta in a defamatory and demeaning way through AI-generated images and deepfake videos. The order came from Justice Manoj Jain in a defamation suit Gupta filed against the party. The posts were reported to have appeared on AAP's official and verified social media accounts. Gupta's plea asked the court to restrain the party from publishing or circulating such content.

According to the plea, the material portrayed her as a liquor vendor, hawker and delivery agent and as head of a fictitious scheme called "Har Har Rekha or Ghar Ghar Theka Yojana." One video allegedly showed her serving drinks to men at night, while another showed AI-generated figures of her and the Deputy Chief Minister pouring liquor and ice cubes. Gupta's plea said the videos looked so real that they created a misleading impression of her involvement in selling and serving liquor. The court noted that one video posted on X on November 4 had reportedly drawn about 75,000 views, 1,600 likes and 470 reposts when its screenshot was taken.

Justice Jain said that the offensive portrayal of the Chief Minister through AI-generated videos could not be treated as permissible political satire. He distinguished healthy criticism and humour from content that attacks personal dignity, and said the posts in question crossed that line by being defamatory and offensive to a woman holding constitutional office. He added that satire may hurt an individual but cannot be allowed to cause irreparable harm to dignity or reduce a person to an object of ridicule. The court also observed that holding public office invites greater scrutiny, yet does not permit the compromise of an individual's dignity.

Referring to earlier decisions, including the Raghav Chadha case, it said that until legislation regulates AI-generated content, courts must examine whether such use infringes the right to dignity. The court issued notices to all defendants, including AAP, and listed the matter for further hearing on December 4, 2026. The articles do not report any response from AAP to the order or to the allegations. They also do not say whether the content has already been removed from the platforms.

Articles.Title: Delhi HC orders takedown of AI-generated videos targeting CM Rekha Gupta

stories.Headline: NCS programme doubles reach, bringing AI and coding skills to more lower-income pupils
stories.Summary:
NCS gave more than 130 primary pupils from lower-income families hands-on lessons in artificial intelligence, coding and robotics on Oct 31 at its NCS Hub in Ang Mo Kio. The event was the largest edition yet of N-Able Me!, the company's flagship corporate social responsibility initiative, and it marked a doubling of the programme's reach in its fourth year. The pupils, all in Primary 3 to 6, took part in practical sessions rather than traditional lectures. The programme aims to narrow the digital divide by giving children from lower-income families early exposure to technology.

The curriculum included a three-hour Micro:bit workshop in which pupils learned coding basics and worked in teams to build simple games. Each participant took home a Micro:bit device to support learning beyond the event. At a Superhero AI and Robotics Booth, children used an app developed by NCS employees to create AI-generated images of themselves as superheroes pursuing their dream jobs. A 1½-hour AI masterclass introduced foundational machine learning and prompt engineering, and robotics activities let pupils see hardware engineering up close.

NCS said the programme was run by a team of company tech volunteers and supported by strategic partners including the Ministry of Social and Family Development, ComLink+, Yayasan MENDAKI and The Straits Times School Pocket Money Fund. Senior Minister of State for Social and Family Development and Home Affairs Goh Pei Ming, the guest of honour, encouraged the participants and presented them with completion certificates. Goh said that when government, community and corporate partners work together, children can be given a better start. NCS chief executive Sam Liew said technology should be an inclusive enabler whose benefits reach everyone.

The pocket money fund, started in 2000 by The Straits Times, provides financial relief to children and youth from lower-income families and has helped more than 230,000 cases to date. Under the scheme, primary pupils receive $65 a month, secondary students receive $100 a month, and those in ITEs, junior colleges and polytechnics receive $125 a month. Liew said the aim is to equip young people with foundational tools so they can see themselves as builders in the AI era. The articles do not say whether the programme will expand further or when the next edition will take place.

Articles.Title: NCS programme doubles reach, bringing AI and coding skills to more lower-income pupils

stories.Headline: Home-based patient care among AI applications being tested at next-gen 5G, 6G research centre
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, the National University Health System (NUHS), telco Singtel and telecommunications equipment maker Ericsson signed a memorandum of understanding to open a research centre testing AI healthcare on 5G-Advanced and 6G networks. The centre is exploring a future in which hospital patients recovering at home are watched by wearable medical devices that detect dangerous changes, such as a sudden spike in blood pressure or an abnormal heart rate. If the readings point to an emergency, hospital staff and emergency services are alerted in real time. NUHS chief executive Yeoh Khay Guan said the partners hope to turn future telecommunications technology into practical healthcare applications. NUHS runs hospitals including National University Hospital, Ng Teng Fong General Hospital and Alexandra Hospital.

The partners say current 5G may not cope with the larger data loads expected as more patients recover at home, patient data becomes more complex and AI tools generate more data. The newer networks are expected to handle those volumes, with 5G-Advanced launched in 2025 and 6G slated for commercial launch in 2030. According to Singtel, the newer networks will be faster than current 5G and have much lower latency, meaning they respond more quickly. Chau Yuen, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University, said 6G is predicted to support a much larger number of connected devices. Because more processing can move to the cloud, devices such as augmented reality headsets could be made smaller and less bulky.

Yeoh said the planned uses include autonomous mobile robots for logistics and patient care, internet-connected devices for home care and support for surgeons during operations. NUHS plans to replace its Microsoft HoloLens headsets, which surgeons use to view a holographic image of a patient's heart from CT scans, with slimmer augmented reality glasses. Gao Yujia, director of the new National University XG AI Centre, said better networks and AI could place the hologram on a patient more accurately than is possible by hand now. Gao also said that no AI deployed on 5G so far can give hospital-wide recommendations, and that such systems have worked only at small scale, such as on a single ward. NUH is already testing nursing robots, which are meant to help nurses handle an expected rise in patient numbers rather than replace them.

Articles.Title: Home-based patient care among AI applications being tested at next-gen 5G, 6G research centre

stories.Headline: Redefining Investment Advisory in the Age of AI
stories.Summary:
On 2 November 2026, Forthright Securities, a Hong Kong brokerage under JF SmartInvest Holdings, took part in the Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK event at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre as a first-time exhibitor and Gold Sponsor. The company's pitch was that as its AI tools grow more capable, its human advisers matter more. The article is a paid post produced by the advertising partner, published on 5 November 2026, and the event opened on 2 November with more than 45,000 participants from over 120 economies. Regulators used the week to announce new measures on artificial intelligence applications and governance, tokenisation and payment connectivity.

The company's main product is the Forthright Smart Investment Terminal, a tablet aimed at experienced individual investors. It combines AI-powered analysis, real-time market support monitoring and analytical tools with the firm's investment research, while the human adviser handles questions the models cannot settle. The firm says its three most-used AI features, AI Assistant, Market Monitoring and Portfolio Analysis, have each been used by more than 80 per cent of clients. On the opening day, the Securities and Futures Commission set out plans for principles-based guidance on AI applications with greater autonomy, focused on safety and preserving human accountability and oversight.

Richard Zhengwei He, chief executive of Forthright Financial and Forthright Securities, spoke at a session titled "Agentic Alpha: The Future of Dynamic Wealth." He said agentic AI is goal-based and expects it to change how financial institutions work with clients in the short term. In the longer term, he said he sees no inherent conflict between financial institutions and agentic AI, which he described as bringing reliable, understandable and suitable guidance to people previously excluded from the financial system. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, speaking at the opening session, said the city has become the world's largest cross-boundary wealth hub, with net inflows to its asset and wealth management industry up roughly 200 per cent last year.

The article describes the wider context as a shift in how Hong Kong investors trade, with 95 per cent of the city's stock investors now trading online, according to the Investor and Financial Education Council's latest study. The company describes itself as a licensed brokerage that opened a four-floor flagship investor experience hub in Sheung Wan in July 2026 and gained virtual asset business qualifications in May 2026. The article does not say what the firm plans next beyond continuing to pair its AI tools with advisers. The text is promotional and carries a risk warning stating that AI analyses are for reference only and do not constitute investment advice.

Articles.Title: Redefining Investment Advisory in the Age of AI

stories.Headline: PARAMOUNT, the First Randomized Trial of AI-Enabled Plaque-Based Care, Meets Primary Endpoint in Late-Breaking Results at AHA 2026
stories.Summary:
The most recent article, dated November 7, 2026, reports that PARAMOUNT, the first randomized trial comparing artificial intelligence guided plaque-based care with usual care, met its primary endpoint. Cleerly, a company that specializes in advanced cardiovascular imaging analysis, presented the primary results as Late-Breaking Science at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The trial compared care guided by AI-based quantitative coronary CT analysis with usual care based on stress testing. The article indicates that the AI-guided approach improved diagnostic certainty and led to more patients receiving lipid-lowering therapy. The trial enrolled patients across multiple sites, and the article notes that 2,600 patients were randomized to receive care based on the AI analysis, with the remaining participants assigned to usual care.

The primary outcome was a measure of diagnostic certainty, which the article describes as improved in the AI-guided group. Lipid-lowering therapy rates were higher in the AI-guided arm than in the usual care arm, according to the reported results. The article does not provide a full list of secondary outcomes or safety findings. The article attributes the presentation to Cleerly and quotes Todd Callahan, identified as a leader in the company, who said the findings show that clinicians who use the technology can make more confident decisions about patients. Another quoted commentator, identified as a cardiology researcher, said the results support broader adoption of the technology in routine practice.

The article also reports that the company stated the trial was designed and conducted with independent oversight, though the article does not name the oversight body. Contact details for Cleerly's communications team appear in the article's sidebar. The article places the results in the context of ongoing debate over how best to evaluate coronary artery disease and whether coronary CT analysis should replace or supplement stress testing. It does not describe any regulatory decision, reimbursement change, or guideline revision that would follow from these results. Further peer-reviewed publication of the trial, and further analysis of its secondary endpoints, are not described in the article as scheduled.

Articles.Title: PARAMOUNT, the First Randomized Trial of AI-Enabled Plaque-Based Care, Meets Primary Endpoint in Late-Breaking Results at AHA 2026

stories.Headline: Phishing Has a New Target: The AI Assistant Reading Your Email
stories.Summary:
Security researchers have warned of a new phishing technique that targets AI assistants that read and summarize employees' email, rather than only the people reading it. The technique, called prompt injection, hides instructions in an email that the assistant processes but the recipient never sees, such as in HTML comments, invisible text, or encoded content. One example observed in the wild, presented as a routine recruiting message from a well-known brand, contained hidden instructions written for an email assistant. Those instructions told the assistant to forward the message to colleagues, keep the hidden content attached to each copy, and search the mailbox for cryptocurrency wallet material to send to an outside address.

The article explains that such attacks can succeed because an assistant often cannot reliably separate the content it is meant to analyze from commands it is meant to obey, since both appear to it as plain text. The attacker in the example needed no link click, attachment, or password entry from the employee. Whether a given assistant complies depends on its safeguards and the permissions it holds. The article also notes that summaries can strip away context, such as an unusual sender address, that employees normally use to spot suspicious messages, and that a message labeled urgent by an assistant may draw more attention.

The article's author, Merium Khalid, Director of AI & Automation at Barracuda, recommends that organizations treat external email as potentially malicious data and never as a source of commands. Suggested measures include stopping malicious messages before they reach inboxes, removing hidden elements before content reaches an AI system, and deploying detection for instruction-like language in email. Organizations should also limit assistant permissions so they cannot forward to distribution lists or send to external addresses, and require human approval for financial transactions, vendor changes, and bulk sending. The article says no single control will stop every variation, so these protections should be layered and updated as attacks evolve.

Articles.Title: Phishing Has a New Target: The AI Assistant Reading Your Email

stories.Headline: The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking
stories.Summary:
Vals AI has published results from its Vals CyberOffense benchmark, which tests whether AI agents can break into simulated corporate networks without human help. Each agent works alone from an isolated Kali Linux machine, starting only from a public web address, and every action is logged and scored automatically. The best result came from GPT-6 Sol, part of OpenAI's restricted Daybreak cyber program, which reached 80.8 percent of its objectives. The freely available open-weight model Deepseek V4.1 Flash came close at 72.8 percent, at roughly $3 per run compared with about $22 for GPT-6 Sol.

In the harder Lighthouse test, GPT-6 Sol Daybreak took admin control of the first company, stole passwords, and used them to break into the second company, completing 27 of 31 objectives in under three hours. Deepseek V4.1 Flash completed 21 objectives at a tenth of the cost and was not limited solely by safety guardrails. The researchers also found that longer runs matter a great deal, since Deepseek scored nothing in its first 25 million tokens and made most of its progress only after 100 million tokens. Vals concludes that short tests therefore underestimate what open models can do. Once a model's weights are public, the researchers note, no provider can control or restrict how it is used.

Vals says the same findings could help defenders, because models that can exploit vulnerabilities can also help companies find and fix them first. The firm expects attacks on real networks to increase in the coming months. The results match a July analysis by the UK's AI Security Institute, which found the gap between open and closed frontier models in cyber capabilities has shrunk to four to seven months, down from six to ten months for most of 2025. That analysis also found open models far cheaper to run, with a Deepseek V4-Pro cyber-range run costing $1.19 compared with $85 for Anthropic's Opus 4.5, and said the safety measures on open models proved largely ineffective. A separate Anthropic study reported that the freely available model GLM-5-3 can build exploits at nearly the same level as Anthropic's internal top model, Mythos.

Articles.Title: The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking

stories.Headline: Canada AI Health Strategy [2026]: $100M Plan, Privacy Gaps
stories.Summary:
Canada's federal government has announced a $100 million plan to make health information, including imaging, medication records and vitals, more accessible to AI researchers, and privacy specialists are warning about the risks. According to CBC, the funded platform is called Vital, and it is part of the national AI for All strategy that Prime Minister Carney launched on June 4, 2026. The health mission within that strategy focuses on AI for diagnostics, patient care and system efficiency. Vital is designed to give trusted researchers at Canadian universities or research institutions access to the data.

Under the plan, datasets will not include names, birth dates or health insurance numbers. Researchers will reach the records through a web portal separate from the rest of the internet, which keeps the data inside a controlled environment. Studies will also be reviewed after publication for sensitive information. Dr. Amol Verma, a physician and co-leader of Vital, said research data needs to be de-identified or anonymized and governed carefully to protect patient privacy. The reporting makes clear that these steps are the safeguards the project must meet.

Dr. Sheryl Spithoff, a physician and assistant professor at the University of Toronto's Department of Family and Community Medicine, warned that algorithms can analyze anonymous data in ways that may be biased against people who share certain characteristics. Her concern is that harm can reach whole groups even when no individual is identified. CBC also reports that the federal, provincial and territorial privacy commissioners issued a joint resolution on responsible AI in health care. That resolution sets six principles: privacy protective, valid and reliable, safe, human rights affirming, transparent and accountable. It also warns of unauthorized use of personal health information, inaccurate inferences and systemic discrimination.

CBC's reporting includes a claim that proposed legislation could let private companies use patients' medical records without their knowledge or consent. The available sources do not identify the bill or provision involved, so that claim is not confirmed. Readers should keep that claim separate from the Vital platform, which as described limits access to trusted researchers. The sources also do not say when the review of published studies will take place or how often the portal will be audited. Those details, along with the outcome of the legislative question, remain open.

Articles.Title: Canada AI Health Strategy [2026]: $100M Plan, Privacy Gaps

stories.Headline: AI Stocks Diverge as Democratic Election Victory Sparks Rotation Into Cloud Giants
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, US technology stocks shifted sharply after the Democratic Party's election victory raised concerns about possible restrictions on new data centre development. Investors moved money toward established cloud computing companies and away from semiconductor makers and firms building additional AI computing capacity. Amazon rose 6.1 per cent, Microsoft gained 6.7 per cent, Alphabet climbed 3.2 per cent and Meta Platforms advanced 1.4 per cent. The gap between companies running existing AI infrastructure and those depending on future capacity expansion became the central theme.

Goldman Sachs reported that both long-only funds and hedge funds were buying major cloud providers, which it described as a clear rotation into hyperscalers. The bank's specialists said investors saw the Democratic win as potentially making new builds harder while increasing the value of existing, power-secured computing capacity. Possible changes to permitting, water use rules, electricity access and tax incentives could make new data centres more costly and slower to build. Goldman suggested that scarcer powered capacity could lift prices and strengthen the position of current operators. Future-capacity providers could be left behind as a result.

CoreWeave fell 9.9 per cent and Nebius dropped 6.7 per cent, while other neocloud providers, data centre builders and chipmakers such as Micron Technology also weakened. Investor Brad Gerstner said on the All-In podcast that regulatory obstacles could keep between 10 and 15 gigawatts of expected 2027 capacity from coming online, figures Goldman noted were already below some industry projections. Gerstner had earlier called about 25 gigawatts a realistic US target in September. Research firm SemiAnalysis flagged 16.7 gigawatts of planned Texas capacity for 2028 as potentially vulnerable, and Goldman warned that the election added political risk on top of forecasts above 30 gigawatts.

Goldman also cautioned that chip demand could outrun the facilities needed to use it, which could turn the semiconductor story into an inventory correction if power and sites lag deliveries. A Financial Times report cited in the analysis said Amazon Web Services had been receiving about $3 billion of Nvidia GB300 server racks each month, with some stored because certain sites lacked enough electricity. The bank further argued that permanently higher infrastructure costs, rather than simple delays, could weaken the economics of AI adoption and reduce competitive pressure on traditional software and media firms. The articles present the rotation as more than a temporary swing between sectors, with investors now weighing which firms benefit from scarce computing capacity.

Articles.Title: AI Stocks Diverge as Democratic Election Victory Sparks Rotation Into Cloud Giants

stories.Headline: AI stock rout: Should Singapore investors buy the dip or cut exposure?
stories.Summary:
A sharp sell-off in US technology stocks has spread to Asia and Singapore, leaving investors to weigh whether to buy the dip, cut their exposure or wait. The Nasdaq 100 plunged 6.4% on Nov 5, two days after the US midterm elections, wiping out about US$2.5 trillion in market value. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 12.2%. Chip-heavy markets in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan were hit on Nov 6, and Singapore-listed technology stocks also took a beating.

The fall followed a Democratic sweep of Congress, which raised the prospect of tighter scrutiny of artificial intelligence. Investors were already questioning how quickly spending on chips and data centres would turn into profits, and experts said crowded AI bets and borrowed money may have amplified the drop as funds rushed for the exits. Investors are watching whether greater scrutiny of electricity and water use, grid costs and permits leads to rules that delay data centre construction. They are also looking at whether major cloud providers trim their spending plans and whether chipmakers cut their earnings forecasts.

Saxo chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said in a note to investors on Nov 6 that AI demand and existing infrastructure had not disappeared overnight, and that many leading technology companies still have substantial cash flows and competitive advantages. She described the change as one in market sentiment and in how investors judge future growth, regulatory risk and acceptable valuations. Brian Levitt, chief global market strategist at Invesco, called the sell-off a reset in one of the market's most crowded trades, warning the correction could continue. He also said lower prices are making some AI stocks more attractive to long-term investors.

Chanana advised that long-term investors who can ride out further losses may keep investing regularly if their holdings still suit them. She suggested those with spare cash focus on firms with strong balance sheets, steady cash flow and reasonable valuations, and spread purchases over time. Heavily exposed investors could shift money towards established cash-generating businesses or other sectors, while those trading on margin should work out how far prices could fall before they must add cash or sell. Afdhal Rahman, executive director of wealth advisory at OCBC, said in a Nov 6 note that cloud giants such as Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are relatively well placed in the near term, while he favours graphics processors, custom chips and networking equipment. He was more cautious about smaller AI cloud providers that rely heavily on debt.

Articles.Title: AI stock rout: Should Singapore investors buy the dip or cut exposure?

stories.Headline: Japan deploys AI, specialist teams to counter cyberattack wave
stories.Summary:
Japan's government on Friday, November 6, 2026, approved a package of emergency measures after a run of personal data breaches caused by unauthorised access. The package was announced at a meeting of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and relevant ministers. It was drawn up after Takaichi asked officials the previous week to prepare it, following a series of high-profile leaks from cyberattacks. One of those attacks hit the internet service provider GMO Internet Group, which was faced with a ransom demand. Public concern about cybersecurity has been rising in the same period.

The package calls for more use of artificial intelligence to find weaknesses in computer systems. It also provides for setting up several teams of highly skilled specialists. According to the report, a rescue team drawn from experts in the public and private sectors will be formed to help businesses hit by cyberattacks with their initial responses. The articles do not give a budget, a headcount or a start date for these teams. They also do not say how the new teams will coordinate with existing agencies.

The articles do not identify any party held responsible for the breaches beyond the attackers, and they do not name any company that failed to protect data. Prime Minister Takaichi is described as having directed officials to produce the package and as leading the meeting where it was announced. The report attributes the measures to the government as a whole, which compiled them with the relevant ministries. Kyodo, the news agency that reported the story, is the named source of the account.

The package responds to a wave of cyberattacks that has drawn attention to Japan's defences, and the articles tie it directly to that wave. The report does not describe what the government will do next or set out a timeline for implementing the measures. It also does not say whether further legislation or funding will follow. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Japan deploys AI, specialist teams to counter cyberattack wave

stories.Headline: Europe’s AI Stocks Are Falling. Is the Selloff Overdone?
stories.Summary:
Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence boom fell sharply on Thursday and Friday, November 5 and 6, 2026, after Democrats won broadly in the U.S. midterm elections. The Nasdaq Composite had its deepest one-day drop in 19 months on Thursday, with the Nasdaq losing more than 5%, and the rout wiped nearly $3 trillion off the market value of S&P 500 companies. On Friday, markets in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan were hit hard, and the Korea Exchange imposed a circuit breaker in morning trading after the KOSPI fell 8.7% at one point. Investors worried that Democratic control of Congress, including wins in some key data-center states, could bring tougher AI regulation and slow the construction of data centers. The selling had started before the election, as chipmakers and neocloud companies helped drive the Nasdaq to its worst October since March 2025.

The drop confirmed the Nasdaq Composite was in correction territory and put it on track for a fourth straight weekly fall. The CBOE Volatility Index logged its biggest one-day jump in about 19 months and stood at 26.07 on Friday. Nvidia had its largest one-day fall since January 2025, when the Chinese model DeepSeek rattled Wall Street, though it rose 3.6% in premarket trading on Friday. Other chip stocks, including AMD, Intel, Broadcom and Micron Technology, were up between 5% and 8.3% in premarket trading. Nasdaq 100 futures were up 1.48% at 4:14 a.m.

ET, while Dow futures were down 0.66%. Anthropic, the AI company preparing to go public, felt the effects directly. CNBC reported that some of its investors had lowered their valuation hopes, with one saying a more likely range was $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion. That compares with a $1.5 trillion figure another investor called a stretch and a recent target of $2 trillion. The investors spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to discuss the matter, and Anthropic declined to comment.

Analyst Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson said investors would expect the deal to price at least at the low end of earlier expectations, and that pricing it well was the best way to set the company up for success. Jane Gibbons, an equity strategist at Jefferies, described Thursday's selloff as reactionary rather than a fundamental reset, driven by worries over AI spending, policy and inflation. Anthropic filed its registration statement on October 26, 2026, and an amended preliminary prospectus on November 2 seeks a listing on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, with the share count and price range still undetermined. The filing shows $17.0 billion of revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026, up 1,127% from a year earlier, while compute and infrastructure expenses grew 382%.

It also discloses roughly $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, about $69.8 billion of which falls due within twelve months. The company had raised $141.1 billion in total and held $95.6 billion in cash, plus $36.3 billion in short-term investments. Its roadshow was still expected to begin in the week of November 9, and a May 28 round had valued it at $965 billion. Meanwhile, an October jobs report due Friday could shape interest-rate expectations, with traders pricing a more than 65% chance of a December hike.

Articles.Title: Japan, South Korea stocks plummet as AI selloff accelerates
