stories.Headline: Immigration Seekers Face Risks Using AI for Legal Advice
stories.Summary:
Documented, a New York City immigration news outlet, published an article on November 6, 2026 warning that AI tools often give incomplete immigration legal advice. The piece draws on a report from the startup Vals AI, which tested the most popular AI models on immigration scenarios and checked their answers against rubrics written by immigration law experts. The article's author, Dara, is a journalist and senior fellow at the American Immigration Council who has covered immigration policy for years. The story points to the growing reach of AI in everyday searches, where a 2026 Pew Research study found that 42% of Americans use AI chatbots to look for information.

According to the Vals AI report, even the best-performing model, a costly version of Anthropic's Claude, gave incomplete answers in most situations, and other models did worse. The report concluded that AI tools should not be relied on to independently advise clients on their specific situation. The article gives two main reasons: AI models are limited by their training data, which may predate recent policy changes, and they cannot tell which details matter, so they may miss facts that change a case. When asked about 2025 and 2026 policy changes, even models that could search the web provided less than a third of the information experts sought. The weakest category was temporary or fragile status, including Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, which are the cases where people face the highest risk of losing status.

The article notes that the report's findings are the author's reading of the Vals AI study and of surveys, not the statements of a government agency or company spokesperson on the matter. A 2025 survey by Rev found that 43% of Americans were comfortable asking AI for help clarifying legal terms, but only 6% would rely on it for an immigration case. The author also cites a 2021 University of Denver study showing that few immigrants with immigration-related problems used the internet as a resource, and many of those who did went straight to agency websites. The article says that only a quarter of closed immigration court cases as of August 2026 had legal representation, which leaves many people with few options beyond online sources. The author's advice is to seek out real immigration lawyers when possible and to rely on trusted expert sources such as free legal clinics and reliable news outlets.

Articles.Title: Immigration Seekers Face Risks Using AI for Legal Advice

stories.Headline: Joe Tsai: Open source helps more people take part in AI development
stories.Summary:
Joe Tsai, co-founder and chairman of Alibaba Group, said at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit on November 3 that open-source AI models can cut research and development costs for small and medium-sized enterprises. He argued they also let developers in emerging economies build AI applications suited to their own countries. His remarks were reported by China Daily, which published them on November 5, 2026. Tsai linked the push toward openness to rising demand for AI applications, which he said is outpacing the supply of computing power. Chinese technology companies, in his account, are stepping up efforts to release their models as open source and to open up their wider ecosystems.

He added that Alibaba has open-sourced more than 470 Qwen models. The move is presented as a way to widen who can take part in building AI rather than leaving development to a small group of firms. Tsai pointed to a nonprofit organization in Uganda as an example of how this works in practice. The group used open-source Qwen models to develop models for local languages, and those models now cover 68 African languages. According to the speech as reported, this helps more people overcome language barriers and make use of AI tools in their own tongues.

The example was offered as evidence that open models can reach communities that commercial products often overlook. The articles provided do not describe any policy changes, deadlines, or formal obligations arising from the speech. They also do not report reactions from other speakers or companies at the summit, or any plans for further releases beyond the figures Tsai cited. Beyond the summit remarks, the source material contains nothing on how the Uganda project was funded or how widely the African-language models have been adopted.

stories.Headline: Dartmouth’s president has evaded Trump so far. Will she outlast AI?
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth College president Sian Leah Beilock has become one of the most prominent academic voices in favor of artificial intelligence, even as other women newly appointed to Ivy League presidencies have left their posts under pressure from the Trump administration. The Boston Globe profile, published in November 2026, describes Beilock as the last woman standing among that group. Her public push includes an essay in The Atlantic in September titled "Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth" and a welcome message to incoming students. Beilock has used her position to advocate for AI on campus at a time when many colleges are debating whether to restrict it.

Under her direction, Dartmouth gave students access to the Claude chatbot through a partnership with Anthropic. In October the college held a three-day conference celebrating Dartmouth as the birthplace of AI, which it says it helped name in 1956. The event included a conversation with a former chief technology officer of OpenAI who is a Dartmouth alumnus. The article notes that the conference was held the day after provost Santiago Schnell resigned, and its theme asked what must remain human. Beilock has also said faculty and students must learn to think alongside AI and have hard conversations about learning in a world where it plays a major role.

The resignation of Schnell, her second-in-command, came after he used AI to write and publish articles, including an opinion piece in The Washington Post and a statement to the student newspaper. A faculty committee Beilock convened reviewed his work and chat logs and found he had violated several Dartmouth policies, especially on academic honesty. Beilock said in a letter that leaders must model the transparency and human judgment they expect from students. She has also said the episode prompted useful conversations about what creation means and how technology can help people think better rather than replace their thinking.

Beilock arrived at Dartmouth in 2023 with a five-point plan covering student mental health, civil discourse, career counseling, carbon neutrality, and innovation. Earlier, she kept her position and kept Dartmouth out of conflict with Trump by meeting quietly with his staff, adopting a policy of institutional neutrality, and declining to sign a protest letter over federal research cuts. Critics on campus argue the school's deal with Anthropic came after the company settled a copyright lawsuit over pirated books, and that open discussion arrived too late. Supporters, including engineering professor Eugene Santos, say universities should explore new technology, and the article does not report further decisions on the college's AI policy.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth’s president has evaded Trump so far. Will she outlast AI?

stories.Headline: Is Your AI Ready to Support a Critical CX Moment?
stories.Summary:
This is a sponsored feature from CX Today, not a news event, so the story is about guidance for customer service operations rather than something that happened on a particular date. Content Guru's Harris (the article's quoted expert, identified only by surname) argues that AI-supported customer service is most tested when outages, extreme weather, or public safety incidents cause demand to spike. The article describes these as the moments when automation faces its hardest test, because organizations must absorb sudden volume increases while making sure customers with urgent problems still reach the right help quickly. It also notes that a critical moment is not always about volume, since emergency services and utilities may receive contacts tied to safety risks or vulnerable customers at any time.

The article sets out what resilience requires. Harris says the service should stay consistent whether it handles one contact or 10,000, with extra compute and tokens added as demand rises but the customer experience unchanged. Organizations should automate high-volume, low-intensity enquiries and free human agents for urgent or emotional cases, and AI must be able to recognize urgency early and route the conversation. Harris says that where even a 0.1% chance of a wrong automated outcome is unacceptable, firms should use a deterministic pathway or capture basic information and pass it to a human. The piece also recommends proactive messaging, such as an SMS alert about an outage, to stop avoidable contacts, and it stresses that CRM and customer data systems must stay available and carry context across channels.

On testing, Harris says organizations should check AI at scale before rollout, generating thousands of use cases that range from satisfied customers to very negative experiences, combined with load tests and scenario simulations of infrastructure failures. Failing to handle urgent requests, giving unsafe guidance, or failing to transfer a customer should count as a failure of the implementation. Harris also advises avoiding vendor lock-in, so that a single model or vendor failure does not disable the service during an incident. Harris's closing point, quoted in the article, is that organizations must plan for the worst even though they hope it won't happen. The article does not describe any specific incident, regulatory change, or deadline.

Articles.Title: Is Your AI Ready to Support a Critical CX Moment?

stories.Headline: The MedTech AI revolution starts with getting the foundations right
stories.Summary:
The Veeva MedTech Summit in Amsterdam, where Oliver Johnson of Med-Tech Insights reported on the event, was the setting for discussions about artificial intelligence in the medical technology industry. The main point was that organisations need sound foundations before AI can deliver results. Speakers argued that reliable data, consistent processes, appropriate governance and capable people matter as much as the technology itself. The article is an opinion-style feature rather than a breaking news report, and it draws on several presentations and interviews given at the event.

Becki Brasher, Regulatory Affairs Director at Medtronic, described a four-year journey in which the company first harmonised processes, improved data consistency, consolidated systems and set up governance structures before adopting AI. She said the company had to earn the right to use AI rather than starting with the technology. The article notes that introducing AI into fragmented environments can produce outputs that are hard to trust, validate or scale. It also stresses that employees need knowledge and oversight to use new tools in their daily work.

The closing keynote, featuring Erik Orzechowski and Benjamin Rochette, focused on how companies can move quickly on AI without weakening quality, safety and regulatory standards. The speakers argued that governance should be built into technology development from the start, with closer collaboration between IT, Quality and Regulatory teams. They also said oversight should be proportionate, so that an AI tool handling low-risk administrative work needs less control than one affecting patient safety. Brasher, for her part, said human judgement should stay in place until trust in AI accuracy is established.

The article places these views in the context of a broader warning that a convincing AI answer is not necessarily a correct one. Speakers compared using AI without understanding the underlying subject to using a calculator without knowing the mathematics, and raised concern about future professionals losing the expertise needed to challenge AI outputs. Suggested next steps include starting with controlled pilot projects, measuring value through time savings, shorter cycle times, less rework, quality and adoption, and keeping governance adaptable as the technology and regulations change. The author says interviews from the summit will be published in the coming weeks.

Articles.Title: The MedTech AI revolution starts with getting the foundations right

stories.Headline: AI in homebuilding: Using AI and ERP systems to make better decisions faster

Swainhart explains that reliable data helps leadership teams respond faster and more accurately to shifts in the market, with examples including tracking home closings and mortgage performance. The interview also looks ahead to what Swainhart describes as the next phase of AI in homebuilding, which centers on intelligent workflows. These workflows are meant to automate routine tasks, improve productivity in the field, and keep important business information connected across the systems that builders depend on.

The article frames these changes as a shift from collecting information to acting on it. The emphasis falls on turning operational records into business intelligence that management can use in real time, rather than on any specific product release or mandated requirement. stories.Headline: AI medical innovations take center stage at 9th CIIE
stories.Summary:
At the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai, a range of AI medical solutions were unveiled and became a main highlight of the expo's medical equipment and healthcare products exhibition area. The technology has moved beyond imaging assistance into surgical navigation, chronic disease management, and intelligent decision-making during medical interventions. The CIIE is described as a key platform for testing AI applications, connecting with hospitals, and speeding up their adoption. The reporting presents these developments as a sign of how quickly the technology is being put to use in clinical settings.

Roche is showing solutions built with ecosystem partners that combine AI and digital tools across the industrial chain, aimed at breaking down data barriers and improving precision in diagnosis and treatment. One tool is a one-stop AI research aid that helps doctors choose topics, review literature, and generate solutions, which the company says will raise research efficiency. Another is a digital remote patient management system that sends follow-up reminders and provides disease education so patients can manage their health at home. Haier's healthcare arm, Incaier, is presenting six AI-driven scenarios, including autonomous labs, autonomous drug management, and proactive health. Incaier also launched an AI strategy built around a central "Incaier brain," and it says its platform serves researchers, healthcare professionals, and patients and already has more than 450 AI-native applications.

Australian biopharmaceutical company CSL signed an agreement at the CIIE with Beijing's Peking Union Medical College Hospital to explore using AI to identify and help diagnose hereditary angioedema, a rare disorder that causes recurring swelling attacks. A hospital representative said the partnership hopes to use advanced AI algorithms to support traditional lab testing and move cutting-edge technology into clinical tools more quickly. The hospital expects this to improve early diagnosis and screening efficiency for clinicians. Philips, in its 2026 China edition of the Future Health Index report released at the CIIE, also highlighted the growing clinical value of AI and the rise of human-machine collaborative medical teams. Philips China's chief regional leader, Liu Ling, said China is actively bringing AI into medical practice and is becoming a leading force in global medical AI applications.

The Philips report found that 95 percent of Chinese clinical healthcare workers surveyed said their focus has shifted or will shift toward higher-value clinical work, compared with a global average of 82 percent. It also found that 81 percent of Chinese patients surveyed believe learning to use AI will become an essential skill for health management, against a global average of 59 percent. In addition, 69 percent of Chinese healthcare workers said they believe AI helps improve patient health outcomes. Taken together, the figures suggest that Chinese respondents are more optimistic than their global counterparts about the role of AI in both clinical work and personal health management.

Articles.Title: AI medical innovations take center stage at 9th CIIE - China Daily

The company says inference, the stage where trained AI models produce results, is becoming a larger share of AI workloads, and this shift is changing how data centers are designed. On the consumer and business side, AMD is highlighting its Agentic PC, which uses Ryzen AI Max Series processors to run large AI models locally. The company says this approach protects data privacy and reduces token costs. Spencer Pan, senior vice-president of AMD and president of AMD Greater China, is quoted as saying that growth in agentic AI is driving continued demand for computing power. He said AMD's full-stack product range, spanning cloud, edge and endpoint devices, along with its open software ecosystem, lets the company work closely with customers, partners and developers in China.

Pan also said AMD hopes to use the expo to combine leading computing technologies with China's varied industrial settings, so that AI can become a strong driver of industrial development. The article places the company's presence within its education efforts in China. Through a program called "Spring Rain," AMD is working with universities to set up AI training labs and innovation demonstration centers that bring its open-source ROCm software and Ryzen AI platforms into teaching and research. At this year's expo, the company is showing university projects, including protein structure research by East China Normal University using the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 processor and a smart home project from Beijing University of Technology. The article does not say what comes next for these products or programs beyond the expo.

stories.Headline: Japan's Nikkei posts 3rd-largest point drop on record as AI-linked stocks tumble - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, Japan's benchmark Nikkei stock index plunged more than 3,600 points, marking its third-largest point drop on record. Artificial intelligence-linked stocks came under heavy selling pressure in Tokyo trading. The sell-off followed renewed worries about tighter regulation after the U.S. midterm elections. The 225-issue Nikkei Stock Average closed down 3,643.13 points, or 5.96 percent, from Thursday, ending at 57,434.77. During the session it fell more than 4,300 points at one point and briefly dropped more than 7 percent.

The broader Topix index shed 232.40 points, or 5.90 percent, to finish at 3,707.99. The Nikkei's close was its lowest since mid-April, and selling spread across nearly all stocks on the Prime Market. Tokyo stocks followed overnight losses on Wall Street, where technology shares fell. Investors there reportedly worried that Democratic gains in the midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data center construction and AI investment. Xinhua's report does not name any specific official or company as responsible for these moves.

It attributes the sell-off to market concern rather than to a formal government action. Analysts quoted by Xinhua said concerns about a possible economic slowdown also emerged as a new factor weighing on the market. That worry broadened the sell-off beyond technology stocks. stories.Headline: AI spending is on the rise, but are companies measuring the right returns?
stories.Summary:
Business leaders are expected to invest an average of $173 million in AI over the next 12 months, according to KPMG's latest US AI Quarterly Pulse Survey, and that rising spending is raising questions about how companies measure what they get back. KPMG argues that productivity gains, the easiest AI benefit to quantify, have dominated the conversation, and that relying on them alone risks missing value in customer relationships, innovation speed, decision-making quality, and new revenue sources. Stanford University's 2026 AI Index reports that 88% of surveyed organizations used AI in at least one business function in 2025. Some of AI's most significant effects may be less immediate or harder to pin down, so they may not appear in short-term financial results.

KPMG suggests treating AI investments as a portfolio rather than a single category, separating use cases that aim for near-term operational returns from those that aim to unlock growth or reshape operating models. The firm offers five questions to test AI value: what business problem the investment is meant to change, what performance looked like beforehand, whether success is about cost, revenue, quality, speed, or customer experience, when a meaningful return should be expected, and whether the project is creating enough value to scale, change, or stop. Matching the metric to the use case means a customer-facing system might be judged on retention or sales, an internal tool on time saved, and a product-development system on speed to market. The article presents this as a way to see more accurately whether each investment is achieving its intended outcome.

The article also points to the people using the technology as a major factor in results. A joint study by KPMG and The University of Texas at Austin analyzed more than 1.4 million workplace AI interactions from 2,597 employees over eight months, finding that the strongest users framed problems carefully, challenged outputs, refined responses, and applied their own judgment. KPMG's Q3 2026 AI Pulse Survey found that 65% of leaders expect AI agents to drive the integration of AI collaboration skills into workflows, and that the share developing role-specific guidelines for working with AI agents rose from 21% to 55% year over year. Shears, who leads KPMG's aIQ program, says it combines AI tools with training and governance, including an aIQ Academy. The article is sponsored branded content, and KPMG's Rahsaan Shears is the source for the company's views throughout.

Articles.Title: AI spending is on the rise, but are companies measuring the right returns?

stories.Headline: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
stories.Summary:
Arjun Panickssery, writing a LessWrong shortform post on December 30, 2023 (the page is dated November 6, 2026), said he struggles to believe that autonomous AI research and development is as ingenious as it is often described. He reported monitoring several side projects in which an AI model, which he called Astra, was used on tasks such as building a new Scrabble engine, a bot for Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, and formalizing proofs for an AI philosophy contest. In each case, he said, the model's judgment was poor in basic ways, and he gave examples of the model missing the most important papers in a literature review, running experiments with too little training data to be informative, and pursuing trivial directions in a long research wiki. He also judged an Apart hackathon, where eight submitted papers were often similar to each other and methodologically incomplete in a way that overlooked the most straightforward analysis. He described one exception, hill-climbing tasks with fast feedback loops, where he improved a Scrabble benchmark roughly tenfold, but only after supplying key ideas himself.

The post's comment thread adds a related picture, and it leans on named evaluations to support it. One commenter, Julian Bradshaw, argued that AI systems perform well when a human points them in the right direction, and that this need for human guidance is still necessary. He cited P-Zero's TasteVal, which reported a breakpoint around December 2025 after which Opus 5.5 reached about 2.30 times human expert compute efficiency, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.15 to 4.37, though only 1.14 times on normalized task score. By contrast, Epoch AI's InnovationEval found that Fable 5 could not reach 5 percent of human real-world innovation gains on an AI R&D task, despite claiming more than 40 percent performance. A third Epoch study, "Can AI automate Epoch?", found that Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra reached only about 65 percent of human Epoch employee performance.

Bradshaw suggested the gap partly reflects task design, since TasteVal specified research problems tractable to known methods while the Epoch tasks required novel ideas or were open-ended. The commenters also disagreed about model quality and about the wider context. Anthony DiGiovanni said that Opus 5.5 was significantly better at clear writing than Astra 6, while Roman Kornev argued that the real change is the amount of steering applied to tasks relevant to AI safety, and pointed to OpenAI and Anthropic research on covert underperformance and persona vectors. The articles do not say how the comment thread concluded, and they do not indicate any further steps or planned follow-up by the author.

Articles.Title: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious

stories.Headline: Interview: China to play key role in advancing Global South media cooperation in AI era, says Bernama chairman - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China is well placed to play a key role in supporting the Global South's media sector through its advances in artificial intelligence, its wide range of international media partnerships and its stated commitment to cooperation, according to Wong Chun Wai, chairman of the Malaysian National News Agency, Bernama. Wong made these remarks in a recent interview with Xinhua in Kuala Lumpur. He said such cooperation could help media organizations adapt to technological change, build their capabilities and gain a better understanding of China through exchanges and firsthand reporting. Wong was in Beijing for the 7th World Media Summit, which runs from November 5 to 9 under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action."

Wong said the rapid growth of AI is transforming the media industry, opening new opportunities for news organizations while forcing them to rethink how they operate. He warned that buying a tool and installing it in a company is not enough, and that businesses must consider how AI could fundamentally reshape newsroom operations. He hoped the summit would give media organizations a platform for practical discussion of AI applications and newsroom change, so they could learn from one another. He also wanted greater attention at the summit to the practical needs of Global South media and to concrete cooperation on technology use and capacity building. Wong urged participants to move past general commitments toward cooperation that produces tangible results.

Wong recalled taking part in the 6th World Media Summit in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in 2024, and said his visit to Kashgar had stayed with him. Visiting the region let media practitioners see it firsthand and compare it with what they had read or heard before. He recalled that some participants, passing cotton fields and seeing machines used to cultivate the crop, described the scene as the real Xinjiang. Wong argued that such visits give international journalists a clearer picture of China, where development keeps bringing change even to places they have already seen. He also stressed the value of accessible, people-centered content on subjects such as tourism, food and how young people live in each country, since China remains a very important topic for Malaysia.

Wong added that China's fast growth in its creative and cultural industries offers lessons for Malaysia as it works to expand its own creative sector. He said he watches a lot of Chinese AI and short dramas to see how the sector is advancing and to learn how Malaysia might do the same. He expressed hope that the 7th World Media Summit would further strengthen cooperation between Bernama and Xinhua. He also encouraged media organizations across the Global South to turn shared ideas into concrete initiatives.

Articles.Title: Interview: China to play key role in advancing Global South media cooperation in AI era, says Bernama chairman - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Xinhua Headlines: World summit highlights transformation and collaboration of global media in AI era - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
The 7th World Media Summit opened in Beijing on November 5, 2026, and runs through November 9. Organized by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing Municipal People's Government under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action," it brings together nearly 500 representatives from close to 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government bodies, the United Nations and other international organizations across 112 countries and regions. Delegates are weighing how media can use artificial intelligence without losing credibility, and how they can move from competition toward cooperation. Coverage of the event describes the gathering as a response to an era in which seeing is no longer believing.

Speakers at the sub-forums argued that AI is reshaping the global communication landscape, not just upgrading newsroom routines. Hervé Azoulay of the Silk Road Business School in France said digital cultural content has become a source of international influence, pointing to the global reach of Chinese web novels, drama series and video games. Per Markus Andersson, CEO of Sweden's Aeon Media Group and editor of The Nordic Times, said AI now lets a small team do work that once required hundreds of people, including research, translation and content production. Tian Weigang of the Communication University of China described AI's growing role in smartphone photography and news gathering. Ofiul Hasnat, editor-in-chief of Daily Finland, warned of misinformation, privacy breaches, algorithmic bias and digital inequality, and urged media to adopt the technology very cautiously.

Responsibility was a central theme, with speakers repeatedly saying that AI's limits begin where journalistic professionalism takes over. The co-editor-in-chief of Germany's Junge Welt questioned who controls the technology and whose interests it serves, and said his paper's principle is that human beings write for human beings. Bridgid Nzekwu of the Press Association Academy in Britain said her agency uses AI for transcription, archive retrieval and data screening but never to generate content. Marek Traczyk, chairman of the Polish Media Association, argued that AI can assist verification but cannot replace source-checking or the separation of facts from interpretation. Kamel Mansari, editor-in-chief of Algeria's Le Jeune Indépendant, called unconditional reliance on automated content editorial suicide and urged transparency and labeling of AI-assisted material.

Speakers from the Global South and smaller nations said they want to help shape the rules of emerging technology rather than simply receive them. Viasen Soobramoney, CEO of South Africa's Independent Media IOL and the African News Agency, said African stories have too often been told through outside perspectives, and that the continent must take part in the development and governance of these tools. Aminath Namza of Public Service Media in the Maldives asked whether ordinary people are being prepared equally. Abdul Hakim of Indonesia's Antara News Agency said that technology makes media faster and intelligence makes it smarter, but trust makes it matter. Speakers also praised the summit itself as a platform for dialogue, with Sarwar Kashmeri of Polaris-Live.com in the United States calling it especially important at this moment.

Articles.Title: Xinhua Headlines: World summit highlights transformation and collaboration of global media in AI era - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Potential Sciences, an AI startup building large-scale chemical data sets, secured backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund, as part of an eight-figure raise (Joel Khalili/Wired)
stories.Summary:
Potential Sciences, a British startup that uses artificial intelligence to speed up drug design, launched on November 5, 2026, and announced seed funding in the tens of millions of dollars. The company is backed by SovAI, the UK government's AI venture capital fund, and by Twin Path Ventures, among other investors. The founders declined to disclose the precise figure or the company's valuation. The startup plans to build large chemical datasets by simulating interactions between atoms, small molecules, amino acids and proteins using basic physics.

The company's aim is to train AI models that can predict how drug candidates will behave in the human body, so that unpromising molecules can be ruled out before reaching the lab. Its founder and CEO, Hatem Helal, argues that this approach would lower the cost of experimentation and could make it economical to develop treatments for rare diseases. He describes the goal as more bespoke medicines tailored to individual biology. The article notes that a large share of AI drug discovery work relies on a single public database, the Protein Data Bank, which Helal says is too small to train sufficiently advanced models. Potential Sciences is therefore relying on synthetic data generated through simulation.

Helal said the company wants molecules that will not work in the clinic to fail quickly, and he described the broader aim as improving predictions of how molecules interact with human biology. Academic experts quoted in the article were cautiously positive. Peter Wolynes of Rice University said the approach would likely be an improvement but described current protein engineering as far behind where it needs to be. Alan Fersht of the University of Cambridge said he was optimistic that accurate interaction calculations would eventually revolutionize drug development. Joséphine Kant, head of ventures at SovAI, joined the startup's board and said its physics-based approach and access to computing resources set it apart.

The article places the company within a crowded field that includes Basecamp Research, Isomorphic Labs and CuspAI, and it says SovAI was established earlier this year with roughly $800 million and access to the UK's national AI supercomputer. Wolynes also cautioned that designing a drug is far less of a bottleneck than the testing needed to establish safety and effectiveness, so treatments will still take a long time to reach patients. The article also raises the risk that the same tools could be used to design dangerous chemicals, and Helal acknowledged that concern. The company has not yet decided how it will earn revenue or whether it will make its models freely available.

Articles.Title: Potential Sciences, an AI startup building large-scale chemical data sets, secured backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund, as part of an eight-figure raise (Joel Khalili/Wired)

stories.Headline: Forget six fingers. AI’s bigger story is quantity
stories.Summary:
Ten thousand AI agents were set loose on an open problem in mathematics, whether the equations of fluid flow always behave, and within four days they produced a proof that specialists are still debating. The same lab then posted more than 700 manuscripts at once, each result costing only a few hours of machine thinking. The writer, Nilesh Jasani, founder and portfolio manager of GenInnov Asset Management in Singapore, argues that this flood of results, rather than the old complaints about errors, is now AI's most important story. The article describes a tool that rewrote a half-million-line programme into a new language in 11 days, a job its creator estimated would take three expert engineers a year. The same article says another model found thousands of unknown security flaws in major operating systems within weeks, one of which had hidden from human auditors for 27 years.

A genome atlas predicted the effects of all nine billion possible single-letter changes in human DNA. Jasani also cites an AI system that proposed about 380,000 stable crystal structures, compared with roughly 20,000 found in all of human experimentation. He notes that the maintainers of curl ended their bug bounty after a flood of poor AI submissions, though their later reports were largely accurate but overwhelming in volume. Jasani's central claim is that institutions built for a trickle, such as peer review and court dockets, cannot cope with this volume, and he says the quality debate offered remedies that quantity does not. He writes that human attention, trust and time do not grow exponentially the way machine output does.

He also argues that the physical world is the last brake, so whoever controls the final physical step holds a veto over the many intellectual steps before it. For businesses, he expects continuous and compounding disruption, with many gains arriving as ordinary costs quietly disappearing. He warns that organisations unable to sort, verify and act on abundance will fall behind. The article is an adaptation of a piece first published on GenInnov's blog, and it frames the present as the last comfortable moment before a tsunami becomes visible. Jasani concludes that quality was the question people knew how to argue about, while quantity is the one they will have to live with.

Articles.Title: Forget six fingers. AI’s bigger story is quantity - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Equinix opens SG6, its sixth Singapore data center, with liquid cooling for AI workloads
stories.Summary:
Equinix, the digital infrastructure company based in Redwood City, California, announced on November 6, 2026 that it has opened SG6, its sixth data center in Singapore. The facility is designed for artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and other data-intensive workloads, and it adds to Equinix's global network of more than 280 data centers. The company says the site gives customers the infrastructure they need to connect, innovate and scale as AI-driven demand grows. SG6 is located in a市场 the company describes as one of the most strategically connected in Asia-Pacific.

The facility is among the first built under Singapore's Data Centre Call for Application framework. It uses advanced cooling, including proprietary systems and liquid cooling, to support power-hungry GPU equipment. Equinix says SG6 is designed to reach a Power Usage Effectiveness of 1.20 and is targeting Green Mark Platinum certification. The building also includes rooftop and facade solar panels, rainwater harvesting and lower-carbon construction materials. The company links the project to its sustainability goals of net zero emissions by 2040 and 100 percent renewable energy coverage globally by 2030.

Adaire Fox-Martin, Equinix's chief executive and president, said the company has invested in Singapore for nearly 25 years and called the city one of its most important markets worldwide. Cyrus Adaggra, the company's president for Asia-Pacific, said the region is at the forefront of digital transformation and that SG6 will help customers expand across the area. Equinix has said its Singapore data centers have had 100 percent renewable energy coverage since 2020. The company also described the initial investment of about $290 million, which provides 8 megawatts of capacity and roughly 1,550 cabinets in the first phase.

Equinix entered Singapore in 2002 and has grown from one facility to six, and it says its Singapore sites connect to more than 17 subsea cable systems. The company also plans to open a Co-Innovation Facility at SG6 in 2027, in partnership with the National University of Singapore, to research cooling, energy storage and related technologies. Upon full build-out, the SG6 site is expected to offer up to 20 megawatts of IT capacity. The articles do not say more about the timing of that build-out.

Articles.Title: Equinix Opens SG6 in Singapore, Expanding AI-Ready Capacity in One of Asia-Pacific's Most Connected Markets

stories.Headline: Kos Biotechnology Partners Announces Investment in Fathom Therapeutics to Advance Novel, AI-Driven Drug Discovery Platform
stories.Summary:
Kos Biotechnology Partners, a global life sciences investment firm based in New York and Athens, Greece, announced on November 6, 2026 that it has invested in Fathom Therapeutics. The investment was made through Kos BioVentures, the firm's first life sciences fund, as part of Fathom's Series A financing. Sutter Hill Ventures led the oversubscribed $55 million round, which also drew other leading investors. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire.

Fathom Therapeutics is a drug design company that applies quantum chemistry, physics-based molecular simulation, and artificial intelligence to find new small molecule medicines. Its proprietary Microcosmos platform combines these methods to predict how proteins move and how they interact with drug molecules at atomic resolution. The company says this approach could help reach biological targets that have been considered difficult or impossible to drug. The financing is intended to help Fathom scale the platform, advance its internal pipeline, and expand its partnerships.

Fathom's chief executive is Dr. Huafeng Xu, a pioneer in computational drug design, and the company was co-founded by Yujie Wu, its chief technology officer, and Jesús Izaguirre, its chief computational scientist. Dr. Simos Simeonidis and Alex Tzoukas, the co-founders and managing partners of Kos, praised the company's expertise in quantum chemistry and AI and said the firm believes the technology could change how medicines are discovered. Xu welcomed the Kos team to the investor group and said the company looks forward to working with them. The release says the team includes scientists behind the Anton supercomputer and widely used computational methods for predicting protein-drug interactions.

The release places the investment within Kos's broader strategy of backing therapeutic technologies, differentiated drug discovery platforms, and globally competitive biopharmaceutical companies. Kos says it manages $125 million in assets and invests across all stages of development in therapeutic breakthroughs, biodefense, and tech-enabled pharma services. The announcement does not disclose the size of Kos's own stake or the valuation of Fathom. It also does not describe specific clinical milestones or timelines for the company's drug candidates.

Articles.Title: Kos Biotechnology Partners Announces Investment in Fathom Therapeutics to Advance Novel, AI-Driven Drug Discovery Platform

stories.Headline: “AI will generate nearly half of network traffic by 2035”
stories.Summary:
Nokia published its Global Network Traffic Report on 4 November 2026 from its base in Espoo, Finland, forecasting that artificial intelligence will drive nearly half of global network traffic by 2035. The company says networks will increasingly have to serve connected machines as well as people, with AI pushing up demand for uplink capacity, faster response times and processing closer to users and devices. It expects total traffic to nearly quadruple from 2026 levels to almost 3,789 exabytes per month, with 44% of that driven by AI. DCD, republishing a piece from SDxCentral two days later, put overall growth at 28 percent a year and the AI-native share at roughly 1,681 exabytes per month.

The report breaks the AI figures down further. Traffic generated directly by AI applications and workflows is forecast to rise 60-fold from this year's level, at a 58 percent compound annual growth rate, reaching 987 exabytes per month or 26 percent of global traffic. Another 694 exabytes per month, or 18 percent, is expected to come from AI-influenced traffic such as extra video consumption or online shopping. Agentic AI traffic is projected to grow about 160-fold to 585 exabytes per month, a 76 percent rate, while physical AI traffic from robots and robotaxis is set to grow 105-fold to around 67 exabytes per month, a 68 percent rate. Physical AI is expected to send more than 90% of its traffic over the uplink by 2035.

Most AI traffic is expected to stay in the central cloud, but edge and metro core infrastructure is projected to carry 36% of AI-native traffic by 2035, with the edge handling nine percent and the metro core 27 percent. Nokia links this shift to more efficient models, low-latency needs and data sovereignty requirements, which it says will support a more distributed setup it calls the AI grid. Enterprise AI traffic is forecast to grow at a 59 percent rate, faster than consumer AI, with industrial IoT devices such as cameras, drones and sensors producing about 70 percent of it. Beyond AI, the report says fixed wireless access will account for more than one-third of consumer cellular traffic by 2035.

Pallavi Mahajan, Nokia's Chief Technology and AI Officer, said AI is changing what networks must provide, not only how much traffic they carry. She argued that networks built for traditional internet applications will have to support machines that need real-time responses and strain the uplink, and that network readiness should be central to AI planning rather than an afterthought. Nokia also warned that rising uplink demand will stress cellular networks, noting that latency and jitter begin to climb once a cell's uplink utilization passes 70 percent during busy hours. The report rests on a bottom-up model of consumer, enterprise and AI traffic, combining application usage, device activity and agentic workflows with third-party research, expert review and Nokia lab testing.

Articles.Title: Nokia: AI will equal half of all network traffic by 2035
